articles.title: Nicaragua Deportation Story
articles.author: Becca Renk Foster, John Perry
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On 1 October 2026, Jeffrey Isaac Jarquin, a 35-year-old Nicaraguan man, was deported from the United States by ICE and, on arrival in Managua, was immediately sent to prison by Nicaraguan authorities. Reports described him as a “torture victim,” a “political prisoner,” and a “prominent figure in the anti-government protests” that occurred in Nicaragua in 2018. His story was covered by the Washington Post , CNN , ABC News , The LA Times and other outlets. It featured on Democracy Now and he received support from the former head of Human Rights Watch, Kenneth Roth . Not one of the reports, however, investigated Jarquin’s role in those “protests” nor recorded that in November 2018, he was found guilty of various acts of terrorism and sentenced to more than 16 years in prison. “Tortured” or “torturer”? Who is Jeffrey Isaac Jarquin, the man being championed by corporate media? In April 2018, protests began in Nicaragua which were part of a U.S.-led and funded coup attempt . Since the protests were ostensibly “student-led,” several universities in Managua were occupied and used as command centers by paid criminals whose financing originated from USAID and the National Endowment for Democracy. In May 2018, the authorities of Nicaragua’s free National Autonomous University (UNAN) announced that it had been forcefully occupied by outsiders. One of these was Jarquin, known colloquially as El Nene (“The Baby”). Anti-government groups were filmed in the university carrying firearms and using its facilities to make explosives . During the occupation they fired at vehicles carrying government supporters on a neighboring highway, wounding several (one, Carlos Sanchez, testified from his hospital bed). They also burned down university buildings, including the nursery . Photographic evidence collected afterwards showed in detail the destruction of the UNAN and the weapons recovered there. President Daniel Ortega, speaking on July 19, 2018, described the UNAN and other occupied universities as “torture centers.” The university students’ union later made a detailed denunciation , pointing out that their leader had been left for dead by opposition thugs. Jeffrey jarquin (standing) at his trial in Managua (Photo El 19 Digital) Arrest, conviction and amnesty Jarquin was soon arrested and in November 2018 was convicted, along with eight others, of damage and destruction of the UNAN facilities, burning down the childcare center, blocking traffic and disturbing public order, robberies with intimidation, using university building 68 to torture people whom they considered infiltrators, and carrying illegal firearms. Although Jarquin was later sentenced to over 16 years in prison, he served only nine months. In June 2019, Jarquin was released along with 55 other prisoners in a general amnesty for those who committed crimes during the coup attempt. The amnesty, however, was conditional: if released prisoners re-offended, they were subject to being put back in prison to carry out their original sentences. Asylum seeker A year later, Jarquin was briefly detained by Nicaraguan police on suspicion of selling drugs. He then seems to have made his way to the U.S. southern border as an undocumented migrant and claimed asylum. In early 2026, U.S. authorities rejected his asylum claim, following which he was subject to a deportation order. Selling passports During his time in the U.S., Jarquin advertised his services in helping Nicaraguans obtain legal residency and political asylum as well as selling Nicaraguan passports , which he bragged about publicly on X (see photo). On February 13, 2026, Jarquín was arrested in Miami and charged with battery following an alleged assault in Little Havana. Although the case didn’t proceed, Jarquin was transferred to ICE custody and deported. Deficiencies in reporting We do not pretend to pass judgment on Jeffrey Jarquin and certainly do not condone the way that he and other migrants have suffered at the hands of ICE. It should also be noted that, of more than 6,000 Nicaraguans deported to their country so far this year, the vast majority have been welcomed by Nicaraguan authorities on their arrival and helped to return to their families. Rather, our argument is about the way that the reporting of Jarquin’s case reflects the unquestioning attitudes of corporate media in its coverage of Nicaragua. Every one of the reports had two glaring deficiencies. First, Jarquin’s portrayal of himself as a torture victim was accepted as fact, something that would not have occurred without further investigation if his claims had related to the U.S. or to another Western country. Yet, while Nicaraguan opposition media (in most cases, funded by U.S. agencies) have convinced human rights bodies to accept the torture narrative as true, there was plenty of contrary evidence from the time when Jarquin was in a Nicaraguan prison. Related: “Guaranteeing Peace & Security”: Nicaragua’s Tourism Sector Backs Proposed Reforms For example, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, Nicaragua’s own human rights commissioner, and a Nicaraguan parliamentary commission all separately investigated torture allegations in 2018, inspecting prisons and interviewing “political” prisoners. All found no truth in the claims after their visits, even though the IACHR changed its stance later. Second, reports on Jarquin’s case ignored plentiful evidence that Nicaragua’s universities - including the UNAN - were used as torture centers by the opposition. The Grayzone’s Max Blumenthal, the first international journalist to report from Nicaragua after the coup came to an end in July 2018, visited the UNAN, interviewed displaced students and photographed the destruction : “Western media paints Nicaragua’s opposition as basically peaceful, democratic victims of unprovoked repression. I visited UNAN today, a public university in Managua they occupied & ransacked. They burned this campus childcare center before they were driven out by police on 7/13.” The violence at the UNAN was hardly exceptional. A detailed critique of Amnesty International’s reporting on the Nicaragua coup attempt, Dismissing the Truth , provided detailed evidence of killings and torture by opposition operatives and contrasted their findings with false testimony in Amnesty’s reports. As authors, we have met torture victims ourselves and verified their claims . Related: Nicaragua’s Fight for Palestine: From Defying the U.S. to Challenging Germany at the World Court Manufacturing consent There is therefore no excuse for lax reporting by media such as the Washington Post, CNN or the LA Times. There is even less excuse for the biased analyses presented by what international lawyer Alfred de Zayas calls “the Human Rights Industry” , because the key organizations have been sent detailed refutations of their reports by groups such as the Nicaragua Solidarity Coalition . But it seems corporate media are willing participants in helping to manufacture consent for regime change in Nicaragua, knowing that they have successfully persuaded their readers that it is a “brutal dictatorship.” At a time when Nicaragua’s sovereignty and its revolution are under increasing threat, propaganda like that surrounding Jarquin’s deportation can be expected to increase.

articles.title: New French Revolution
articles.author: Dennis Broe
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The high-school student protest here in France, whose epicenter is the region’s second largest and most diverse city Saint Denis, is every day gathering steam and sometimes forcing the Western corporate media to course correct after their initial slandering of the event. Rather than depicting crowds of students taking to the new barracks—the blockades around their schools— The New York Times initially gleefully ran a video of a burning trash can, as the symbol of this mobilization, implying the demonstrators were violent terrorists. The protests in the high schools, have now spread to universities, and engulf not just the students but also unions, teachers and their parents and grandparents, all come not only to support the protests but also to protect their children and grandchildren from what are the actual terrorists, Macron’s police. The omnipresent banners tell the story about what the students want and what they are reacting to: overcrowding in the schools with teachers who retire or can no longer take the strain not followed by new teachers— “My mother replaces some teachers in burnout but who will replace my mother?”; the call for the state to deal with the problem of underfunding by means other than repressing demonstrators, that is, those who call attention to the problem— “fric non flic,” that is money for education not police; and the unevenness of money spent where those outside Paris and the central cities are more highly underfunded— “Equality does not stop at the gates of the city.” The signs of burning garbage, widespread on American social and corporate media are the mainstream representation of the students’ protest at their future being torn away from them through lack of funding after nine years of Macron’s austerity budgets while also rewarding the richest with major tax breaks. The disparity between the actual protests and how they are being covered also returns to the way the original French Revolution was experienced in the bourgeois media, not as a first attempt at a people’s liberation but as degenerating into what was called “The Terror.” These emblems, emblazoned in young minds in Charles Dickens’ A Tale of Two Cities, are regurgitated in today’s bourgeois media where property, even garbage cans, is sacred while the protestor’s are returning to the French writer Proudhoun’s retort, “Property is theft.” Related: The World Cup, the LA Olympics and the Death of Sports Innocence And indeed, the largest protest with leagues of students swarming the square occurred this week at the Bastille, the sight of the beginning of the 1789 Revolution. It was here, at the birthplace of the Revolution, that students acknowledged this heritage by singing “Le Marseillaise,” originally sung on the fly as workers’ militias marched from Marseille to Paris to meld with the Parisian street revolt. Trump has called the protests communist and muslim inspired, claiming these are the twin threats that will bring down America from within, a magnificent and astounding case of projection since the force that is most likely to bring down America from within, the true fifth column, is the Trump family and the Trumpists. Later in the week, with the protests creating an inexorable movement, The Times covered them with a degree of fairness but inserted above their coverage another story about overwhelming French debt hastening an increase in the price of French bonds and making borrowing more difficult for the state. The statement being that there really is no choice other than austerity, no matter what the street may say. On Tuesday afternoon Marine LePen, who leads in the presidential polls to be held next April, unveiled her own proposed budget, a complete sop to the wealthiest corporations, as she proposes to cut approximately $154 billion from the French state. This is as opposed to the other alternative which is frequently advanced and just as quickly dropped of a two percent tax on the wealthiest to maintain France’s social services. Related: Media Watch: The Scandals Behind the Scandals The protesters, since they are still majority high school students, have also called much-needed attention to the Macron government’s standard tactic for dealing with the unrest caused by his government’s transfer of wealth upward, and that is with fierce police violence. A 15-year old’s hand was blown off and 16-year old is now blinded in one eye, most likely struck by an LBD riot gun. Over 5000 mostly high-school students have been arrested and many then held in detention. Students are also upset about another Macron “efficiency innovation” and that is the installation of a Elon Musk-type computer application titled Parcoursup which now handles and supposedly systematizes university applications. The system is slow in getting back to students about whether they have been accepted or rejected while also being accused of favoring those from the wealthiest and best-connected schools. The problem is accentuated by the opaqueness of the system. Nobody knows what criteria it uses in a selection that in France is absolutely crucial in determining the future course of a student’s life. Saint Denis Mayor Bally Bagoyoko protecting students The protests have also been the occasion for accusations against the most popular left party, LFI, claiming that the party and its leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon instigated the rebellion. A popular accusation on the right and center-right, fearful that the second round of the next election could pit the far-right’s Marine Le Pen against LFI’s Mélenchon. The charge has been refuted, even by the centrist Le Monde, no friend of Mélenchon, which claimed in an article on its origins that this was a spontaneous uprising. Where the LFI has been important and where it might make significant gains come next April when many of these students will have reached voting age, is in safeguarding the protestors. A local hero of this revolution is the LFI mayor of Saint Denis Bally Bagoyoko who showed up on the picket lines and put himself in between the police and the demonstrators. Bagayoko is of Malian ancestry and a strong supporter of that country’s, along with Burkina Faso and Niger’s, assertion of its sovereignty in kicking out French troops. He is also a critic of French attempts to recolonize the country, an indication that the revolution on the streets of Paris, its environs and across the country has a global resonance.

articles.title: Foreign Policy Undermines International Law
articles.author: Nicolas Davies
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On October 9th, the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize Was awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African international lawyer who defended Nelson Mandela and the anti-apartheid political prisoners on Robben Island, and went on to serve as a judge on the UN International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court (ICC), then as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. In 2025, Navi Pillay led the UN Commission of Inquiry that confirmed that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza. With the world in the grip of seemingly intractable war and chaos, the Nobel Committee clearly wanted to honor someone who has worked against the tide of militarism and violence to uphold international law. And yet, on the same day, the United States unveiled unilateral, illegal coercive measures or “sanctions” against the ICC, where Navi Pillay served as a judge from 2003 to 2008. The UN General Assembly’s 2026 general debate in September also set out to uphold the UN Charter and international law, and to confront the reality that the UN system is failing in its most basic responsibility, to maintain international peace and security. The foundational rules of the UN Charter are that countries must resolve disputes peacefully and refrain from the threat or use of force. But in the General Assembly debate, even as leaders recognized the urgent need to finally enforce the UN Charter, after decades of impunity for aggression and war crimes, they were reluctant to explicitly address the central role of the United States in undermining the rule of international law. Many US allies loyally condemned Russia’s violation of the UN Charter against Ukraine. But none of them even tried to square their singular focus on Russia with the inconvenient truth that their own ally, the United States, has systematically violated the UN Charter for decades, against Grenada , Nicaragua , Panama , Yugoslavia , Afghanistan , Iraq , Haiti , Libya , Somalia , Syria , Yemen, Venezuela , Cuba , Iran and other countries. Related: The Urgency of Recognizing the Ansar Allah Government in Yemen While US allies remain silent, US officials accept no responsibility or accountability for the violence and chaos they unleash, and instead keep doubling down on their failed imperial ambitions and military approach to international disputes, the very antithesis of what the UN Charter requires. Many other leaders spoke out, but without explicitly naming the United States. Algeria’s foreign minister, the veteran diplomat Ahmed Attaf, pointedly asked, “What sort of international order can function properly when principles are selected according to the identity of those who violate them? What confidence can remain in international law when the aggressor is granted the right to self-defense, while the victim is required to justify even the right to survive?” So it is left to the officials of the countries the United States threatens or attacks to remind the world which country is illegally threatening them, as Cuba’s Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla and Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian did clearly and accurately at the General Assembly. Many other leaders made strong statements condemning Israel’s war crimes and genocide in Gaza, even as they neglected to condemn the essential US military and diplomatic role in them. King Abdullah of Jordan described Israel’s objective as “to make a viable Palestinian state impossible,” through “a system of subjugation… de facto annexation… forced displacement… (and) war crimes.” “We have tools,” he reminded his colleagues, “Sanctions, asset freezes, embargoes, diplomatic isolation. And we have a record of using them elsewhere… The question now is: Will we act?” Another of the UN’s tools is the power of the president of the UN General Assembly to convene Emergency Special Sessions (ESS) that can pass “uniting for peace” resolutions. This allows the General Assembly to act decisively on international problems when the Security Council fails to do so, wielding the kind of tools that King Abdullah outlined. The General Assembly’s 10th Emergency Special Session on “Illegal Israeli Actions in Occupied East Jerusalem and the Rest of the Occupied Palestinian Territory” began in 1997, and has been reconvened more than twenty times. In 2022, the 10th Emergency Special Session voted to ask the International Court of Justice (ICJ) some legal questions about the Israeli occupation, which the court answered in 2024, in a finding that the Israeli occupation is illegal and that Israel must “end its unlawful presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory as rapidly as possible,” and “evacuate all settlers.” The next meeting of the 10th ESS in September 2024 passed a resolution demanding that Israel comply with the ICJ ruling and withdraw from the occupied territories within a year. However, the 2025-6 General Assembly president, Annalena Baerbock of Germany, allowed her entire year as president to pass without reconvening the 10th ESS even once. This allowed Trump and Netanyahu to seize the initiative and subject the people of Gaza to a new phase of the genocide under Trump’s Orwellian “board of peace,” a smokescreen for a war of attrition to keep killing civilians and making life intolerable for the people of Gaza, as they struggle to survive in the rubble of their bombed and bulldozed homes. Many leaders at the General Assembly spoke of the urgency of reforming the Security Council, but the greatest leverage they have to achieve that is the General Assembly’s ability to act in an Emergency Special Session when the dysfunctional, corrupted Security Council fails to do so. Nowhere in the world is such action more urgently needed than in Palestine. And yet the 10th Emergency Special Session has not met since June 2025. Now that Bangladesh’s Dr. Khalilur Rahman has taken Baerbock’s place as President of the General Assembly, he should reconvene the 10th Emergency Special Session to take the concrete actions for Palestine that people all over the world are calling for. South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the ICJ is also important, but South Africa has slowed down the already tortuous pace of international justice by requesting 18 months to respond to Israel’s defense against genocide charges. Surely South Africa and the court can find a way to move faster, with the fate of an entire people in the balance. The Genocide Convention was intended to prevent and stop genocide, not just to pass judgment over mass graves and scattered refugee camps. Related: Stop the War Machine: Start Rebuilding America Many people justifiably fear that the United Nations and its institutions are simply too weak to enforce the laws of the UN Charter and the Geneva Conventions and hold the United States and Israel accountable for their crimes. But there was another event on September 16, 2026, which suggests that Benjamin Netanyahu and other US-allied war criminals might want to think twice before assuming that the United States will always shield them from accountability. The week before the General Assembly met in New York, an international war crimes court in The Hague sentenced former Kosovo president Hashim Thaçi to 25 years in prison. The court found Thaçi and three other former leaders of the US-backed Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) guilty of 96 murders, 303 charges of torture, 49 charges of criminal cruelty and 385 cases of arbitrary detention, committed during the US-NATO war on Yugoslavia in 1999. The Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that tried Thaçi, was established in 2011, in response to a Council of Europe Parliamentary Report titled “Inhuman Treatment of People and Illicit Trafficking in Human Organs in Kosovo.” That report detailed extraordinary allegations unearthed by Carla Del Ponte, who was the Chief Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), which were then investigated for the Council of Europe by Swiss state prosecutor and member of parliament Dick Marty. The report substantiated allegations that the KLA transported civilian prisoners from Kosovo to Albania and imprisoned them in a clinic known as the “Yellow House,” where they murdered them and extracted their internal organs to sell on the illicit organ transplant market. As the court records show, these were only the most startling of Thaçi and the KLA’s crimes. The KLA also shot, tortured or beat to death dozens, or maybe hundreds, of civilian prisoners whom it labelled as “traitors” or “collaborators,” during and immediately after NATO’s illegal war to detach Kosovo from the remaining territory of Yugoslavia. While no Americans were charged in these crimes, the CIA and other Western intelligence agencies had worked with the KLA since at least 1996, as it terrorized Serb civilians and attacked and killed Yugoslav police to provoke repression against the Kosovar Albanian population. The escalating violence in Kosovo provided the pretext for a war in which the United States and NATO dropped 23,000 bombs and missiles on Yugoslavia, targeting and destroying vital civilian infrastructure as well as military targets. Then they invaded and occupied Kosovo and built a huge US military base, Camp Bondsteel, which the US also used as a secret prison during its “war on terror.” US Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was so personally invested in the march to war in Kosovo that Time dubbed it “Madeleine’s War.” Albright shunned the traditional political leaders of Kosovo’s independence movement, and instead embraced Hashim Thaçi and the KLA as the United States’ and NATO’s main allies in Kosovo, despite their well-known links to organized crime and heroin smuggling . Related: Are US War Crimes Trapping the World in an Endless Cycle of War and Chaos? With Thaçi at her side at the Rambouillet conference in France, Albright delivered her coup de grace to Yugoslav President Milosevich: an ultimatum that would have given NATO the right to militarily occupy all the remaining territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Milosevich’s refusal to surrender his country’s sovereignty served as the final pretext for the US and NATO to violate the UN Charter in an illegal war that set a precedent for US invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq and the endless wars and chaos that have followed. At the UN General Assembly on September 23rd, Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić thanked the 107 countries that still refuse to recognize Kosovo’s unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia in 2008, and he placed NATO’s war on the remains of Yugoslavia in 1999 squarely at the root of the violence and chaos afflicting the UN and the world. “...the order based on respect for the UN Charter and the law founded upon it no longer exists,” Vučić said. “It was destroyed by those who tore apart the territories of other countries for the sake of their own political and economic interests. They did so unscrupulously, recklessly, and shamelessly.” So is it already too late to try to enforce the rules of the UN Charter? Has the world simply failed to learn the lesson of 1945 that “might makes right,” coupled with the destructive power of modern weapons, can only create a world plagued by endless war and chaos? Or, now that we are staring that world in the face, will we finally heed that lesson and make different choices? It has taken 27 years for justice to catch up with Hashim Thaçi, but, as King Abdullah said, the world’s governments have the tools to enforce the rules of international law if and when they choose, and that is true even in the case of US allies like Thaçi and Netanyahu. But Abdullah’s question remains: will the world’s leaders choose to use the tools at their disposal? First to free Palestine, but also to give our own children and grandchildren the chance to build a peaceful, sustainable world out of the militarism, war and chaos that is the global legacy of a generation of American leaders.

articles.title: Defending a Non-Existent International Law
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Margaret Kimberley, BAR Exec. Editor & Senior Columnist September 30, 2026 Black Agenda Report The Hague Group’s goal is to “. . . take coordinated legal and diplomatic measures against Israel’s violations of international law.” But international law was never a reality. This columnist was honored to be invited to a United Nations High Level Meeting In Defence of International Law called by the Hague Group, which was held on September 25, 2026. Defending and protecting international law is surely a priority for anyone who claims to be concerned about the human rights of all people and the rights of all nations to be truly sovereign. The Hague Group was founded on January 31, 2025, when eight nations: Bolivia, Colombia, Cuba, Honduras, Malaysia, Namibia, Senegal, and South Africa united in The Hague in the Netherlands to take “coordinated legal and diplomatic measures” against Israel’s violations of international law. But if international law had ever really existed the world would be made up of independent nations in control of their own destinies instead of being under control of the colonizers. Yet at the very moment this meeting was held, the United States has increased coercive measures against Iran as part of a war of aggression it waged along with Israel. It is impossible for Iranian airlines to fly outside of that country, just one part of the U.S. “D-Day” pressures on a nation it attacked. The Donald Trump administration has publicly committed itself to destroying the International Criminal Court (ICC) , “brick by brick,” by sanctioning its staff and judges and pressuring those nations that did sign on to the Treaty of Rome that brought it into existence to renounce their membership. It is quite commendable that South Africa stepped forward in 2023 to charge Israel with war crimes at the International Court of Justice and to join with Malaysia in chairing the United Nations meeting. This is work that must be done if the words international law are to have any meaning. The work of the Hague Group is absolutely necessary, but there are also many contradictions to be addressed. The United Nations is an appropriate venue for such a discussion, but the UN is also complicit in bringing the principle of international law to such a low point. UN Security Council Resolution 2803 , passed on November 17, 2025, was one of the more ignominious acts to ever take place at that institution. Resolution 2803, falsely referred to as a Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict , gave the United States’ so-called Board of Peace control over Gaza in violation of the United Nations Charter and of the rights of the Palestinian people. Palestine is not the only scene of a United Nations crime. The 2025 Security Council Resolution 2793 called for a Gang Suppression Force in Haiti, but the existence of paramilitary groups labeled as gangs is the end result of the UN undermining Haiti’s sovereignty with its Core Group and a variety of occupations and interventions over the decades. How then can the United Nations be a venue to discuss the threats to international law? The United Nations Security Council permanent members shirk their responsibilities and go along with the dictates of the United States because their strategic interests are not as different as we are led to believe. Of course, vassal states France and the United Kingdom vote along with their patron. But China and Russia often fail to live up to their perceived status as U.S. adversaries and take the path of least resistance when they have the power to say “no.” Both Russia and China made eloquent statements against Resolution 2803 in 2025 but ended up abstaining instead of using their veto power to scuttle a corrupt arrangement that violated the principles they are sworn to uphold. Gaza is now firmly in the hands of Israel and the United States, the two nations most responsible for war crimes against the Palestinian people, and therein lies the problem for any call to defend international law. There cannot be a meaningful process of upholding international law if the violations currently being committed are unaddressed. In the absence of a determined international commitment to call the violators to account, high-level meetings will be of little use. There also must be clarity and naming of the culprits who wage these attacks. The United States and its NATO junior partners and Israel are international rogues, thumbing their noses at the rest of the world and making a complete mockery of international law. The U.S. has the ability to destroy the ICC even though it was never a member and actually passed legislation, the American Service Member Protection Act , aka the Hague Invasion Act, giving itself the right to forcibly release any U.S. service member from ICC custody. The purpose of dismantling the ICC is to protect Israeli officials from prosecution. The indictments of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and a former defense minister have been ignored by ICC member states, in deference to and fear of the two rogue states. Netanyahu repeatedly flies over the airspace of ICC member states in defiance of the membership they apparently don’t take very seriously. Perhaps the Hague Group should have called their gathering a High-Level Meeting to Oppose U.S. and Israeli Criminality. Although such a name would imply a level of seriousness that simply doesn’t exist. Those two countries are the elephants in the room when one speaks of violations of international law. The president of the United States addressed members of the General Assembly with an explicit threat against Iran, a U.N. member nation. “Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope?” The U.S. is unique in its determination to protect what it sees as its interests, while Russia and China have the power to take action but instead go along in hopes that they can placate a country that is devoted to their destruction. Before the 81st General Assembly meetings began, the United States refused to give visas to Palestinian delegates, in effect banning them from exercising their right to participate at the United Nations, when they had been invited. Trump or any U.S. president can withhold visas, make threats to member nations, and violate the U.N. Charter with complete impunity. If the United Nations lived up to its charter, both the U.S. and Israel would have been expelled long ago. Delegates may engage in performance when they walk out as Netanyahu speaks, but he has no reason to fear as long as Trump or any other presidential partner in crime backs him up. The Hague Group has an important job and a duty to live up to its mission as millions of people have learned to be skeptical even as they would like to be more hopeful that international law will actually exist. Unless the international community finds ways to stand up to the two rogue nations, calls to protect and defend international law will be for naught, a tragic waste of precious time, as continued complicity and fake opposition will rule the day. -Margaret Kimberley is the author of Prejudential: Black America and the Presidents . She can be reached via email at margaret.kimberley@blackagendareport.com. PHOTO: Ronald Lamola, South Africa’s Minister of International Relations and Cooperation at the Hague Group’s UN meeting. articles.title: Venezuela: Don’t Call It Treason.
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Raffaele Timperi September 24, 2026 www.resistenze.org Caracas’s gold is on its way to New York, and Israeli consulates are reopening [in Venezuela] after seventeen years. Those on the left who are searching for the exact moment of the “betrayal” are avoiding the real question: what was “21st-century socialism”? On September 23, from the podium of the 81st United Nations General Assembly, Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, thanked Donald Trump “for his willingness to resume diplomatic relations and cooperation with Venezuela,” and took credit for “the recent binational agreement between the United States and Venezuela, one of the largest ever signed,” intended to contribute “to the energy balance of the hemisphere and the international economy.” She was speaking in New York, the very same city where Nicolás Maduro has been on trial in federal court since January. Maduro was not mentioned even once throughout the entire speech. Five days earlier, on September 18, the Financial Times reported the deal moving 31 tons of Venezuelan gold, worth approximately $4 billion, from the vaults of the Bank of England to the New York Federal Reserve. Delcy Rodríguez’s interim government gained legal control of the gold: it could not sell it immediately, but could use it as collateral for loans. Three weeks earlier, on August 29, Trump had announced from the White House “the largest oil deal in history”: twenty-five years, seventeen fields, approximately 65 billion barrels under US control, a fifth of the world’s proven reserves, with the Pentagon as a shareholder through a private company. On August 30, a thirty-year contract was signed for the Choco gold mine in El Callao with Heeney Capital and Mercuria. On August 11, Caracas and Tel Aviv reestablished consular relations that had been severed by Chávez in 2009, after an Israeli team intervened in the post-earthquake relief effort and an AIPAC delegation was received in the capital. It wasn’t a right-wing government installed by the occupiers that signed all this. It was the PSUV. It was Maduro’s vice president, sworn in as interim president on January 5, two days after 150 US planes bombed the north of the country and Delta Forces removed Maduro and Cilia Flores from Fort Tiuna and transferred them to a federal court in New York. Twenty-nine days later, the same president signed the law privatizing the oil industry. The alibi of betrayal. The prevailing reaction among a certain Italian left has been the reiteration of a tried-and-true pattern: betrayal. They search for the exact moment—the signing in August, the law in January, the swearing-in on the 5th—as if searching for an original sin. It’s the method the communist movement should have learned to discard long ago. All variations of betrayal, from the crudest to the most elaborate, treat a political experience as a legacy to be preserved and its history as a sequence of deviations from an original intention: reflection becomes limited to the search for the moment of rupture, which becomes a moral fault even before it becomes a political fact. No one denies that turning points exist. What is denied is that reading them as an original sin helps us understand the material reasons why a historical process went in one direction rather than another. Betrayal is a consoling category: if the problem is men, the model remains valid. If Delcy Rodríguez betrayed, then “21st-century socialism” was right and must only be purged of traitors. It is the ideological operation that allows numerous organizations that refer, more or less directly, to communism to continue to cite that formula in their programs while its adopted homeland hands over its gold reserves to the US Federal Reserve bank and its gold deposits to the Pentagon. Defending the model, after all, does not mean defending Caracas: it means defending the political line that that word has legitimized here for twenty years. What has never been expropriated? In concrete terms, “21st-century socialism” has been this: a government won through elections and installed within institutions that have never been touched, the same army and judiciary as before, and generous social spending paid for with the proceeds of mining and energy nationalizations. No property relations have been overturned. The factories, banks, and lands have remained where they were, and with them the class that owned them. One only had to look at what was happening in 2020. On the eve of the parliamentary elections that December, to secure the support of opposition parties, the government was cutting wages and allowing Venezuelan capitalists to undergo mass layoffs. The PCV had just left its alliance with the PSUV and formed the Popular Revolutionary Alternative; in response, it was excluded from televised debates and accused by the governing party of “playing the right’s game.” A redistribution based on rent, which had not touched the capitalist basis of economic relations, showed its weakness there: rent would only have to shrink for wages to pay, and the bourgeoisie would once again be the ally to be sought. Six years later, the PCV—which has since been judicially stripped of control of its party symbol—is the only organized force denouncing “the new and grave confiscation of the national patrimony carried out by the illegitimate triumvirate,” accomplished “behind the backs of the Venezuelan people, without transparency, and outside of constitutional controls”: a “wild plunder” disguised as “technocratic rhetoric.” And it does so without aligning itself with María Corina Machado. Those who weren’t in government don’t have to explain today why the government signed: that’s the whole point of class independence. There was no rupture, there was continuity. The apparatus that repressed workers’ strikes, criminalized communists, and administered an oil revenue for a decade, fostering the growth of a bourgeoisie within the state, faced with the collapse of the revenue and the January bombings, did what every bourgeoisie does: it sought the best deal with the strongest capital. It hasn’t betrayed its class nature, it has shown it. Campism put to the test. For years, in Italy, Venezuela has been the exemplary case of an entire political position: the idea that there exist “anti-imperialist” capitalist states to be supported as adversaries of Washington. In eight months, that bastion has become the privileged supplier of the US strategic reserve, 41% depleted by the war with Iran, and Israel’s consular interlocutor. It’s not a paradox; it’s the way it works. When you support a capitalist state because it occupies the right square on the chessboard, you end up supporting those sectors of the national bourgeoisie that at that moment have an interest in trading with Washington’s rival. But interest isn’t fixed forever: the balance of power changes, alliances are re-organized, and the same bourgeoisie that yesterday signed in Beijing and Moscow today signs in Washington without having changed its nature one iota. The buyer changes, not the seller. Those who had built their political identity on the geopolitical positioning of that government, and not on an analysis of the production relations that sustained it, must now explain why the bastion signed, and they do so by speaking of capitulation: that is, dismissing as an accident what was the product of that structure. Chávez’s break with Israel in 2009, in the midst of Operation Cast Lead, was among the most praiseworthy acts of that foreign policy. The fact that it was reversible in seventeen years, and reversible by the very hands of his heirs, is a measure of the value of international positions that are not rooted in the class nature of the state that adopts them. No concessions, in any direction. None of this mitigates the impact of the aggression. A country was bombed, its president abducted by commandos and tried in a foreign court, dozens of Venezuelan soldiers and thirty-two Cubans killed, its mineral and energy resources divided by contract, and the proceeds deposited in an account controlled by Washington. This is an act of imperialist war, and it is the model the United States is building for the continent. There is no equidistance to be maintained on this, and the denunciation must be carried to the full, starting with the Italian government and the Italian companies that are already returning to Venezuelan oil fields. But denouncing imperialism does not require inventing a socialism that didn’t exist. Only a materialist analysis of the true nature of the Bolivarian process allows us to understand why it lacked the strength to resist, and why its leadership was recyclable as administrators of the spoils. A power that hadn’t expropriated the bourgeoisie couldn’t call on the working class to defend it, because it had never given them anything to defend except a certain level of income. Cuba, where property relations were effectively overthrown, has maintained a blockade for sixty-five years. The comparison isn’t based on military power relations, which are not comparable: it’s based on one point alone, namely, that there exists a class there that has something of its own to defend, and knows it. A new century hasn’t changed the basic condition: either the working class takes the means of production from the bosses, or it ends up administering their state on their behalf. The assessment we need isn’t on Caracas, but on those here who continue to explain that an intermediate stage must be passed first, that institutions can be administered as long as “progressives” govern them, and that socialism will come later. Those who seek out the traitor aren’t taking stock. They’re looking for a way not to. -This article originally appeared at https://www.lordinenuovo.it/autore/raffaele-timperi/ www.resistenze.org – Resistant Thought – Theoretical Debate – September 30, 2026 – No. 971 The post Venezuela: Don’t Call It Treason. appeared first on MLToday .

articles.title: The Speech of Capitulation
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: Editorial published in Tribuna Popular , newspaper of the Communist Party of Venezuela (PCV): September 28, 2026 Delcy Rodríguez’s speech before the 81st United Nations General Assembly deserves to be examined closely, not only for what she said, but for everything she left unsaid. Rodríguez avoided any direct reference to the US military intervention of January 3, which culminated in the abduction of Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores, presenting those events instead as “a painful ordeal” for Venezuela. According to the de facto a cting president, the bombings were the result of the “strangulation of domestic political life.” What exactly does she mean by this? Is she referring to the authoritarian turn of the PSUV leadership, the conspiracy against popular sovereignty on July 28, 2024, or the escalation of repression over the past two years? And when she speaks of the “intensified confrontation” with the United States, what exactly is she talking about? Those televised spectacles in which the very same leaders who now smile at the aggressors used to tear their hair out, insisting that if the gringos entered Venezuela, our country would become another Vietnam? Well, the gringos came in, and now Rodríguez is thanking them for their magnanimity. To make matters worse, she presented her subordination to Washington as a “political transformation.” The spectacle becomes even more shameful when one recalls that, just one day earlier, at the very same General Assembly, Trump boasted of having directed the military operation against Caracas. Referring to Venezuela’s wealth, he even declared that after a war “to the victor belong the spoils.” Faced with such a statement, the Venezuelan delegation remained silent. There was no response to this humiliation, no forceful denunciation of the military intervention, no public defense of Venezuelan sovereignty. Clearly, those who truly mourn for the country do not reside in Miraflores[the presidential palace]. In a speech riddled with euphemisms, Delcy Rodríguez described the process of handing over the country’s resources to transnational capital as “economic cooperation.” Venezuelans have yet to see even the first contract from the parade of agreements signed over the past several months. In this respect, Rodríguez is a worthy heir to Nicolás Maduro, who institutionalized opacity as a mechanism for managing the country’s resources behind the people’s backs and ensuring the conditions necessary to entrench himself in power. The acting president also announced before the United Nations a “process of democratic transformation,” yet hundreds of workers in Venezuela are still facing judicial proceedings for the crime of demanding their rights. This should hardly surprise anyone. Rodríguez belongs to the same political leadership that for years helped dismantle the rule of law and reduce the Constitution to little more than a stage prop. Her speech follows the same script as Marco Rubio’s, and it is quite simple: there will be no genuine political opening until the conditions for the plunder of Venezuela’s resources have been institutionalized. Business comes first; once everything has been sufficiently tied down, then we will see what happens with democracy. To put the finishing touch on this farce, Delcy Rodríguez invoked Bolívar to remind everyone that sovereignty resides with the people. Of course it does. And that is precisely why it is obscene to invoke Bolívar while auctioning off the country to the highest bidder. The Venezuelan people have the right to reclaim their institutions, to decide over their own resources, to organize and fight for their rights, and to demand accountability from those who have turned Venezuela into an object of negotiation between ruling elites. The legitimate aspirations of the Venezuelan people cannot continue to be sacrificed in order to guarantee the survival of a corrupt and cowardly elite. articles.title: Delcy Rodriguez at the UN: Betrayal Unmasked
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Eduardo Miguel Álvarez Estévez September 25, 2026 I was optimistic enough—though I’m now ashamed of that optimism—to think that Delcy Rodríguez would use her platform at the UN General Assembly to denounce to the world the kidnapping of Venezuela’s legitimate president, Nicolás Maduro. That she would demand justice for the Venezuelans and the 32 Cubans killed in Operation Absolute Determination. That she would recall that she was a disciple of Chávez. That she would honor Bolívar. She did none of that. What she did was confirm, before the entire world, who she really is: an architect of surrender, a master of treason, a woman who has turned opportunism into an art form. What She Said at the UN Delcy Rodríguez took the podium at the UN and announced—without a date or specific conditions—that there will be elections in Venezuela. She said her government has initiated a “political dialogue with sectors of the opposition” to guarantee “equal conditions for all.” She spoke of a “democratic transformation” and a “rebirth of Venezuela.” She did not mention Nicolás Maduro. She did not mention Cilia Flores, who is imprisoned in New York. She did not mention Hugo Chávez, the man whose revolution she claimed to defend. She did not mention the 32 Cubans who died defending the very same palace where she now holds office. But she did mention Trump. She expressed her gratitude to him. She thanked him “for his willingness to get back on the path of diplomatic relations and cooperation.” She described her meeting with the U.S. president as “historic.” And touted the oil agreement as “the largest ever signed.” Betrayal Is No Longer a Hypothesis In January, I wrote that there had been a betrayal. I was called biased. Today, after this speech, there is no longer any possible doubt. Betrayal is not measured solely by what is said. It is measured by what is left unsaid. And Delcy Rodríguez left out the essentials. She remained silent about Maduro’s kidnapping. She remained silent about the invasion. She remained silent about the dead. She remained silent about Chávez. She remained silent about Cuba. What she did was thank the executioner. The very same Trump who ordered the operation that killed 32 Cubans and dozens of Venezuelans. The very same man who has Maduro in a Brooklyn prison facing charges of narco-terrorism. The very same man who promised to “administer” Venezuela and take its oil for himself. And she thanked him. What This Means Delcy Rodríguez’s speech at the UN is the final confirmation of surrender. It is not a democratic transition. It is a capitulation. It is not a rebirth. It is a funeral. The “dialogue with the opposition” she announces is nothing more than the formalization of an agreement with Washington. The elections “on equal terms” she promises are nothing more than a fig leaf covering the nakedness of submission. And while she speaks of “full democracy” and “reconciliation,” repression continues in Venezuela. Political prisoners remain in jail. The military personnel who refused to comply continue to be persecuted. And the 32 Cubans who died defending the Bolivarian Revolution have not been given a single plaque, a single tribute, or a single word of recognition. She and Diosdado Must Answer Delcy Rodríguez and Diosdado Cabello will one day have to answer to history and to the Venezuelan people. Not to Washington, which applauds them. Not to Miami, which celebrates them. But to the millions of Venezuelans who believed in Chávez. To the families of the fallen. To the Cubans who lost their children defending a cause that these two are now betraying. History does not forget. And traitors always end up alone, surrounded by their masters but abandoned by their people. What I maintain Delcy Rodríguez confirmed at the UN what we already knew: that the Bolivarian Revolution was betrayed from within. That those who claimed to defend it handed it over. That the empire did not need to invade to win: it was enough to buy its way in. Chávez warned us. Fidel warned us. Martí warned us. And we, from our trenches, continue to warn: betrayal is the empire’s deadliest weapon. Not aircraft carriers. Not drones. Betrayal. Cuba has not fallen. Cuba will not fall. But look at Venezuela and learn. Because what happened to Venezuela could happen to us if we let our guard down. Fatherland or Death. We shall prevail. -Eduardo Miguel Álvarez Estévez is a Cuban journalist. articles.title: The Pentagon’s Secret Budget
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By David Vine October 2, 2026 CounterPunch News reports that next year’s U.S. military budget will top out at $1.5 trillion if President Donald Trump gets his way are misleading at best. The true total, if Trump’s proposal passes, could be at least $1 trillion higher. Long before Trump took office, U.S. taxpayers have spent far more on the Pentagon — and its wars — than most know. For decades, Congress, the White House, and the Pentagon have hidden the military’s true cost through little-known bureaucratic practices and budgeting tricks. Journalists, academics, and think tank experts have, with rare exceptions, perpetuated the problem by repeating “official” numbers that don’t come close to telling the full story. Data shows that the budget was already between $1.5 trillion and $1.8 trillion in the last full fiscal year, 2025, as detailed by a recent Project on Government Oversight, or POGO, report I co-authored. Trump’s requests would add another $781 billion, bringing the potential total to at least $2.581 trillion in 2027. The troubling revelation that the government is misleading the public and effectively hiding hundreds of billions in military spending reflects the out-of-control nature of the Pentagon budget. It’s also the only sector of government spending that seems largely insulated from public scrutiny: Imagine the outrage if news broke that the government was hiding hundreds of billions in spending for public housing, Medicaid, or hunger prevention programs. People have a right to know how much tax money goes to military spending. This is critical to debating the proper size of the military budget both on its own and compared to other spending priorities, particularly any program related to education or the social safety net. Understanding the military’s true cost means understanding where and how the government has been hiding the money. Spending Hidden in Other Budgets It’s difficult to untangle how much the country actually spends on the military in part because Congress pays for the armed forces and wars from many budgets rather than one. Beyond the agency controlling the military branches that Trump calls the “Department of War” (the official name is still the Department of Defense), hundreds of billions of dollars are effectively hidden in the budgets of at least 17 other government agencies and entities. In total, each of these additional sums are larger than what Congress appropriates for every non-military agency. For years, TomDispatch and a small but mostly ignored group of budget experts have warned that tota l military spending is far higher than reported . Our new POGO report consolidates this prior work and five different methodologies for calculating the true military budget. The report shows a consensus that military spending was at least $1.5 trillion , with three of five methods reaching similar estimates of $1.7 trillion to $1.8 trillion. The newest of the five methodologies provides the easiest way for anyone to see the hidden spending. The methodology uses data from a government website, USAspending.gov, the product of a 2006 law requiring the government “to give the American public access to information on how their tax dollars are being spent.” The site includes the closest thing to actual spending receipts, making it easier to identify military spending beyond the Department of War’s budget. Let’s take a look at where the money’s hiding. Hidden Nuclear Weapons Costs: $33.8 Billion The most obvious place where Congress and the executive branch hide military spending is in the Department of Energy’s budget. That’s where taxpayers can find the bill for the U.S. nuclear weapons arsenal, which cost around $33.5 billion in 2025. The Department of War controls and deploys these weapons, and their costs should properly be part of its budget, not rolled into the Department of Energy. While the Energy Department plays a role in overseeing the U.S. nuclear weapons stockpile, putting nuclear weapons spending in the DOE’s budget is like a city putting the costs of its police department’s bullets in its transportation department budget rather than in the police budget. Another $300 million in nuclear weapons spending hides in the budgets of the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board and the Army Corps of Engineers, bringing the total to nearly $34 billion. Hidden Military Personnel (Veterans) Costs: $393.3 Billion Taxpayers spend huge sums on the military in the Department of Veterans Affairs and related budgets. The existence of a separate veterans’ agency is a sleight of hand that leads the public to believe this is not military spending. It is. The only difference is the appropriation of money to still another agency. To recruit and maintain armed forces, any government needs to pay its troops and offer sufficient long-term benefits (such as pensions, medical care in retirement, and survivor benefits) to encourage people to join and stay in a dangerous job that involves the risk of killing and being killed. These forms of long-term compensation are personnel costs, just as much as basic pay, and they should be counted as military spending. If a military fails to spend money to support vets, it’s unlikely to function for long. The Bureau of Pensions for veterans was originally part of the War Department (which was the name until 1947, long before Trump’s rebranding) and its budget until 1849 when Congress transferred the bureau to the Department of the Interior. Funding for the Department of Veterans Affairs adds another $389.8 billion to the USAspending.gov methodology total. Almost $4 billion more in long-term spending on personnel hides in the budgets of the departments of Labor, Justice, and several others. All told, these sums reach a staggering $393.3 billion. Coast Guard and Other “Homeland Security” Costs: $16.8 billion Spending for an entire branch of the military, the Coast Guard, is concealed in the budget of the Department of Homeland Security rather than the Department of War. While DHS controls the Coast Guard during peacetime and the branch plays some non-military functions, the Coast Guard is one of the armed forces and is controlled by the Pentagon in wartime. Excluding non-military activities (such as improving boat safety and cleaning up oil spills), Coast Guard spending adds nearly $14 billion to the total military budget. Additional DHS expenses for programs to counter weapons of mass destruction, radiological preparedness, cybersecurity, and other military spending add just under $3 billion, bringing this total to $16.8 billion. The True Cost of the Department of War: $1.3 Trillion The bulk of military expenditures still appear in the Department of War’s budget, which pays for the armed forces and the rest of the Pentagon’s sprawling bureaucracy, including all the weapons, salaries, some benefits, military construction, fuel, maintenance, operational expenses, and much more. USAspending.gov receipts show the Department of War alone spent $1.273 trillion in 2025. The Pentagon controlled another $480 million in spending that hid in the budgets of the State Department, the U.S. Agency for International Development , and the Department of Transportation. Combined with the $444.8 billion tallied previously, total military spending hits $1.718 trillion. That’s more than double the military budget usually reported for 2025: the $850 billion Congress appropriated to the Department of War. Total Military Spending by Agency (FY2025) Agency Name Net Outlays ($) Department of Defense 1,273,158,423,924 Department of Veterans Affairs 389,755,646,022 Department of Energy 33,538,322,898 Department of Homeland Security 16,798,958,047 Department of Labor 3,277,521,935 Department of State 461,862,025 Department of Justice 385,060,843 Army Corps of Engineers 260,017,630 Armed Forces Retirement Home 137,519,390 American Battle Monuments Commission 103,483,062 U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims 49,662,873 Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board 43,703,554 Agency for International Development 15,504,280 Department of Transportation 2,604,283 U.S. Chemical Safety Board 958,374 Social Security Administration 260,504 Department of Agriculture 0* Executive Office of the President 0* TOTAL 1,717,989,509,643 *No FY2025 spending. However, there was a $1 billion budget appropriation to the Executive Office of the President for “Submarine Security Activities, National Security Council.” The government also funded account line items in the Department of Agriculture budget to support the Air Force and Army. Still Other Costs The $1.7 trillion estimate for last year is conservative and still may be too low. While the War Department budget contains classified funding for the CIA, National Security Agency, and other intelligence agencies, the government may hide more intelligence spending elsewhere. NASA space research involves considerable military work, which could add another $10.5 billion, according to USAspending.gov data. Some would also count $1.9 billion in FBI salaries and expenses found in the Department of Justice budget. Other experts consider much larger expenditures in the DHS budget to be military spending, given that department’s role in protecting the “ homeland ” and the increasingly militarized nature of Immigration and Customs Enforcement as well as Border Patrol . This would add at least $216.9 billion after excluding DHS’s Federal Emergency Management Agency spending. Alternate methodologies also include $211.9 billion in interest payments on the more than $40 trillion in national debt stemming from past military spending and wars. You can add and subtract forms of spending that you think belong or don’t belong in the true total, thanks to the transparency of the POGO report’s methodologies. In total, these excluded sums could add another $441.2 billion to the USAspending.gov method’s prior total of $1.718 trillion for 2025. Growing Opposition to Unchecked Pentagon Spending POGO report’s conservative estimates of the FY2025 budget being $1.5 trillion to $1.8 trillion reveal that the true military budget for 2027 could hit $2.6 trillion if Congress gives Trump what he wants. This includes requested increases totaling $781 billion for just the Department of War ($500 billion), the Iran war ($70 billion), veterans ($144.9 billion), nuclear weapons ($53.9 billion), and the Coast Guard ($12.5 billion), let alone other smaller forms of hidden Pentagon spending. When mind-numbing numbers like these reach the trillions, it can be tempting to think, What does it matter if it’s $1 trillion or $1.5 trillion or $2.6 trillion? It helps me to remember that every single dollar spent on the Pentagon is a dollar not spent on our children, on healthcare, on affordable housing, on efforts to slow catastrophic climate change, and much more. If Congress passes Trump’s full budget proposal, military spending will eat up around 75 percent of the discretionary budget Congress controls. Every dollar spent on the Pentagon is also a dollar more for Trump to continue waging his illegal, disastrous war on Iran and the funds to make good on his threats to attack Cuba and other countries. Advocates for increased military spending will likely insist that more money is always needed, no matter today’s true total. That these Pentagon boosters have cited incorrect figures and helped mislead the public for decades raises serious questions about their credibility and the basis for their seemingly endless demands for more money. Thankfully, there’s growing resistance to Trump’s proposals. Nearly 6 in 10 people nationwide believe even the official $1.5 trillion request is “too high,” according to a recent poll conducted by ReThink Media and the Costs of War Project at Brown University, a nonpartisan research group (where I’m a contributor). And Democrats appear to be listening : They’ve voted against Trump’s budget in unprecedented numbers as it winds through Congress. Some Republicans have also expressed concerns about supporting Trump’s proposal given fears about the rising national debt . There are growin g calls to cut the Pentagon budget by hundreds of billions of dollars without touching salaries and benefits for troops and veterans. This would still leave the country with the world’s largest military budget by far and allow Congress to reallocate the savings to programs that improve the lives of everyday Americans. The public needs a full, accurate accounting of the military. Congress could provide an annual True Total Military Budget that tallies all of the Pentagon’s spending in one place and stop hiding funding in other agencies’ budgets. Until this happens, journalists and analysts can help by explaining the full scale of spending and no longer repeating incomplete totals. As Trump asks for the highest military budget in the history of the world and people continue to suffer the effects of his war with Iran — which has killed and injured thousands, increased the price of gas and groceries , and risks even greater catastrophic harm globally — it’s time to have an informed debate about how much the country really needs to spend on its military. -This piece first appeared on TomDispatch . -David Vine ( DavidVine.net ) is a political anthropologist and the author of a trilogy of books about war and peace including “The United States of War: A Global History of America’s Endless Conflicts, from Columbus to the Islamic State.” PHOTO: An aerial view of the Pentagon, Washington, D.C., May 15, 2023.
