articles.title: “The Law of the Jungle Cannot Be Humanity’s Future”: Cuba at UN General Assembly
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Laura Mercedes Giráldez September 28, 2026 Granma On Saturday—marking exactly 66 years since Commander-in-Chief Fidel Castro Ruz’s first address to the United Nations—Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla, a member of the Political Bureau and Minister of Foreign Affairs, took the same podium. The gathered nations once again heard the island’s denunciation of the “collective punishment” inflicted upon it by the United States government—a crime whose “evident and immediate goal is to induce a humanitarian crisis in Cuba.” Speaking from the podium during the general debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, the Foreign Minister recalled the words spoken back then by the historic leader of the Cuban Revolution, in which he condemned war, colonialism, and the exploitation of countries by monopolies. Regarding the continued relevance of those words, he asserted: “The advance of expansionism, acts of usurpation and conquest, and military and economic aggression are alarming. The United States government’s aim to impose peace through force is absurd and unachievable.” He addressed the genocidal crime of Zionism against the Palestinian people, pirate-like attacks on vessels and extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean and Pacific, military aggression against Venezuela, and the war against Iran. His remarks also included a condemnation of the crisis of identity and relevance that has been imposed upon the UN; he therefore called for making the organization “more democratic, effective, and closer to the peoples.” The truths regarding the genocide against the Cuban people struck the Washington delegation like darts; they walked out of the room the moment they heard how the largest of the Antilles is facing “a multidimensional aggression” by their government—described by Rodríguez Parrilla as “permanent, abusive, and ruthless hostility.” He held the White House responsible for the unprecedented intensification of the blockade, noting that its impact has a human face. “The economic war is directed against the people… It claims lives, causes individual and collective suffering, and breeds anguish. It is not ‘collateral damage.’ It is a policy deliberately designed to strike Cuban families where it hurts most, to hinder their well-being, and to wound the dignity of the people,” he asserted. “The United States government and the State Department… have the shamelessness and cynicism to persist in blaming the Cuban government. The executioner blames the victim,” he remarked. At the same time, he emphasized the threat of using military force against the island—a move intended to “nullify national sovereignty through aggression and economic strangulation.” Speaking on behalf of Cuba—a nation of peace—he addressed key issues of international concern, such as the use of information and telecommunications technologies, the imposition of unilateral coercive measures, and various conflicts around the world. He emphasized the Island’s conviction “that the current course of international relations—characterized by disrespect for international law, disregard for the United Nations, and the imposition of the most powerful nation’s unilateral will upon other countries through intimidation and coercion—is dangerous and unsustainable. The law of the jungle cannot be the future of humanity,” he asserted. _____________________________________________________________________________________________________ Address by Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Cuba, at the general debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. New York, September 26, 2026. Mr. President of the General Assembly: Madam Deputy Secretary-General: In approximately three hours, it will be exactly 66 years since Commander-in-Chief Fidel Castro Ruz delivered a memorable speech from this podium, in which he stated—and I quote: “Let the philosophy of plunder cease, and the philosophy of war will cease as well! Let colonies disappear, let the exploitation of countries by monopolies disappear, and humanity will have reached a true stage of progress!” Yet, the advance of expansionism, acts of usurpation and conquest, and military and economic aggression are alarming. The United States government’s aim to impose peace through force is absurd and unachievable. Fundamental pillars of international law and the United Nations—such as the sovereign equality of States—are under constant attack. Zionism’s genocidal crime against the Palestinian people, pirate-like attacks on vessels and extrajudicial executions in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific regions, military aggression against the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, and the war against the Islamic Republic of Iran are new manifestations of this atrocity. They also reflect the crisis of identity and relevance that has been imposed upon the United Nations—including this General Assembly, the most universal, democratic, and representative body of the international community. We are convinced of the indispensable need to preserve and strengthen the UN, while making it more democratic, effective, and closer to the peoples of the world. As is well known, Cuba faces multidimensional aggression from the United States government—a permanent, abusive, and ruthless hostility that has persisted for nearly seven decades. Since January 2026, this aggression has intensified and become more cruel and dangerous with the imposition of an energy blockade that, through intimidation and coercion, prohibits all countries from exporting fuel to Cuba; this amounts to a naval blockade, classified under international law as an act of war. Through successive measures, the U.S. government has increasingly imposed prohibitions on all countries regarding products and services that cannot be exported or transported to Cuba. More than 7,000 containers have been detained at various ports—many containing food, medicines, and medical devices, or even goods contracted by private Cuban companies. In an extraordinary and unprecedented move, a superpower unilaterally deprives all States of the right to export whatever products they wish to whichever countries they choose, while comprehensively and persistently violating the freedom of trade and navigation. Added to this are the intimidation of businesspeople from various countries, forcing them to abandon their investments and business dealings in Cuba against their will; the obstacles and traps laid to prevent the arrival of entirely legitimate commercial shipments; the pressure exerted to halt the flow of visitors and tourists; and the concerted effort to restrict, as much as possible, Cuba’s legitimate access to financing, technology, and markets. Matters have reached the extreme point where sovereign governments are subjected to unimaginable pressure to forgo medical services—services they themselves requested for the benefit of their populations and which are provided altruistically by Cuban professionals—simply because the U.S. government opposes such cooperation. This occurs regardless of the impact or harm inflicted upon populations left without free, high-quality medical care—deprived, in other words, of a fundamental human right. Last Thursday, while this General Assembly was in session, the State Department convened a humiliating meeting specifically with recipient States to exert pressure and issue threats. As described by the Secretary of State, the official policy of the United States is to shut off every valve, outlet, or means of survival for Cuba. The impact of such an ironclad and ruthless blockade has a human face. This economic war is directed against the people; it falls upon the Cuban population as a whole. It claims lives, causes individual and collective suffering, and breeds anguish. It is not “collateral damage.” It is a policy deliberately designed to strike Cuban families where it hurts most, to hinder their well-being, and to wound the dignity of the people. It is an act of collective punishment—a crime also prohibited under international humanitarian law. The evident and immediate goal is to trigger a humanitarian crisis in Cuba, which also constitutes a crime. The United States government and the State Department have been forced to acknowledge the suffering inflicted, yet they have the shamelessness and cynicism to insist on blaming the Cuban government. The executioner blames the victim. They are following the formula defined by the State Department back in 1960 in the infamous Mallory Memorandum, which established—and maintains to this day—the official policy of overthrowing the Cuban government through economic strangulation and by inflicting extreme suffering on the people via material shortages, hunger, and despair. Just a few days ago, the President of the United States declared from this very podium that Cuba is a failed state. If that were the case, why did they have to impose a fuel blockade? Why did they implement secondary sanctions? Why must they threaten, persecute, and pressure every nation on the planet? The U.S. President also acknowledged that his government is exerting the greatest pressure ever placed on Cuba. Months earlier, he had said—and I quote—”the only thing left to do is go in and smash the place up.” The threat of using military force against Cuba persists—conduct that constitutes a violation of international law and a grave breach of the San Francisco Charter. If it were to materialize, it would constitute a crime of immense magnitude. It would result in the deaths of Cubans and young Americans, as well as massive destruction. We hope it never happens. Cuba would exercise its legitimate right to self-defense with the utmost determination and energy. This aggression is accompanied by a brutal media and cognitive war, directed not only against the Cuban people but also against U.S. citizens and global public opinion. It is characterized by crude and brazen attempts to interfere in Cuba’s internal affairs—which constitutes yet another international crime. We are asked what the United States seeks to achieve with such aggressive conduct—a question that often surprises us, given that representatives of that government have openly declared their objective: to seize Cuba, control the country, and dominate its economy. In other words, they aim to nullify—through aggression and economic strangulation—the national sovereignty for which generations of Cubans have fought since the 19th century: first to achieve it, and—since attaining full freedom in 1959—to tenaciously defend it against the gravest risks, including the threat of a holocaust. U.S. behavior rests on the fallacy—proclaimed early this year—that Cuba poses an unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security and foreign policy of the United States; an absurdity that the government repeats shamelessly. In a futile attempt to substantiate this claim, it floods the media with mendacious accusations through its spokespersons and the publications it commissions and pays for, exploiting the U.S. government’s growing dominance over major communication platforms. The U.S. President himself repeated this fallacy in this very chamber just a few days ago. Any reasonably informed observer understands the fanciful and malicious nature of portraying a developing nation like Cuba—relatively small and with a modestly performing economy—as a threat to the planet’s greatest nuclear, military, technological, and economic power. This Organization and its Member States possess abundant evidence that we are a peace-loving country, of Cuba’s efforts to foster international cooperation, understanding, and the peaceful settlement of disputes, and of the active role we have consistently played in support of the United Nations. Cuba is not a threat; the blockade is! Cuba is not a threat; the blockade is! We have always been—and remain—willing to engage in dialogue with the United States government to seek solutions to bilateral differences based on seriousness, respect, sovereign equality, and adherence to international law, without interference in internal affairs or preconditions. We are open to trade and business relations with U.S. companies, just as we are with those of any other country. We are fully aware of the immense challenge facing our nation regarding its security, its survival, the well-being of its people, and the destiny of the Homeland. We do not face this challenge passively; we do so with firmness and dignity. On this basis, we are advancing a process of change—one that is deeply transforming our economic and social model—anchored in our historical experience. On July 30th, during the Seventh Session of the National Assembly of People’s Power, President Miguel Díaz-Canel stated: “Faced with the complex scenario I have described, how do we persist in building socialism? How do we find the financial and material resources to maintain the Revolution’s social achievements? Just as in previous, particularly complex periods—such as the Special Period, when the economic model was transformed under the guidance of the Commander-in-Chief and subsequently the leadership of the Army General to adapt to challenging external circumstances—in the current context, we have set out to undertake the transformations the moment demands. We are doing so under the guidance of the Party, in a collective and democratic manner, and in consultation with the people, without compromising independence, national sovereignty, or the social achievements of the Revolution.” End quote. At that session, the National Assembly of People’s Power approved an innovative program featuring new practices, economic actors, and concepts. All of this is being carried out within the framework of the current Constitution—approved in a free and universal referendum—and in keeping with the concept of our socialist state based on the rule of law and social justice. As the leader of the Cuban Revolution, Army General Raúl Castro Ruz, pointed out—and I quote—: “The most important thing will be proper and timely implementation, with clearly defined priorities and the conscious participation of the people.” End quote. This process rests on the strength we have successfully built, the potential of our human resources, and the determination to meet the people’s needs with the greatest possible social justice, without wavering in our commitment to defend—absolutely and vigorously—our sovereignty and right to self-determination. We know we have the backing of the international community and the solidarity of millions, including an increasing number of U.S. citizens. This is evident in the repeated displays and statements of support for Cuba and of opposition to abusive aggression. It is expressed in the material aid based on solidarity that our people receive, which seeks to mitigate the enormous damage to the Cuban economy and society. That spirit of solidarity and empathy is also expressed with particular strength among Cubans residing—permanently or temporarily—outside the national territory, and among their descendants, especially here in the United States. Mr. President: We reject the Monroe Doctrine and its corollaries, just as we repudiate any attempt at militarization, intervention, or imperialist domination in Latin America and the Caribbean—a region proclaimed a Zone of Peace in 2014, precisely in Havana. As a small island developing state, we stand in solidarity with our brothers and sisters who share a similar status, and with their warnings regarding the worrying and inexorable advance of climate change. It is necessary to foster more inclusive governance of new information and telecommunications technologies, particularly disruptive technologies such as artificial intelligence. We reject the application of unilateral coercive measures. We express our support and solidarity with each and every nation that is a victim of them. We reaffirm our solidarity with the Government of Reconciliation and National Unity of Nicaragua. We reiterate our support for the inalienable right of the people of Puerto Rico to self-determination and independence. The sister nations of Africa and the Caribbean deserve fair and differentiated treatment, as well as reparations for the horrors of colonialism and the transatlantic slave trade. We reaffirm our solidarity with the Sahrawi people and their right to self-determination. We reaffirm our support for the “One China” principle. We are convinced that the current course of international relations—characterized by disrespect for international law, disregard for the United Nations, and the imposition of the unilateral will of the most powerful upon other countries through intimidation and coercion—is dangerous and unsustainable. The law of the jungle cannot be the future of humanity. It was to prevent such practices, and to promote peace and justice, that the generations before us founded the United Nations and, over the decades, developed and sought to enrich its work. Let us restore its role—while there may still be time—before the United Nations goes down in history as an unrealized dream of great promises. In the year of his centenary, let us trust—as did Fidel Castro Ruz, the historic leader of the Cuban Revolution—that if we fight with determination, a better world will be possible. articles.title: Book Review: Stalin the Collected Works, Volumes 5 and 6
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: Reviewed by Grover Furr October 2, 2026 Iskra Books, a publisher of socialist, communist, and revolutionary publications based in Dublin, London, and New York City, has published volume 5 and volume 6 of the Collected Works of Joseph Stalin, entitled Stalin The Collected Works. Volumes 1-4 have already been published. Iskra has announced that volumes 7 and 8, for the years 1925-26, are due out on November 13, 2026. They offer free PDF downloads of all the books they publish ( https://bookshop.org/lists/iskra-books ). Iskra plans to reprint the thirteen volumes published between 1952 and 1955 by Foreign Language Publishing House in Moscow and halted by Nikita Khrushchev’s anti-Stalin campaign. Why reprint a Soviet edition that is more than 70 years old? Particularly when the texts and the volumes themselves are available on the internet for free download in both English and Russian? The publisher’s page explains it as “allowing readers, activists, and scholars access to these texts which in no small measure defined the course of the 20th Century and continue to have relevance for our contemporary struggles.” Since the end of the Soviet Union a revolution in the evaluation of Stalin’s role has been under way. Nikita Khrushchev’s infamous “Secret Speech” to the 20 th Party Congress of February 25, 1956, has been shown to be a tissue of lies. As the Chinese CP leadership concluded a few years later, Khrushchev attacked Stalin to justify a rejection of important communist principles. In 2000 Mikhail Gorbachev’s lieutenant Aleksandr N. Yakovlev boasted that Soviet socialism and the Party had been destroyed by a successful conspiracy that included himself and like-minded Party members because, he said, the communist movement was just as bad as, if not worse than, fascism. Gorbachev made similar anticommunist remarks after 1991. By this time a badly-needed re-evaluation of the “Stalin era” and of Joseph Stalin’s role had already begun. It had become clear to many that the Gorbachev regime was a continuation of Khrushchev’s anti-Stalin campaign, and that both had been central in the demise of the once-powerful USSR. The period of Stalin’s leadership saw the world-shaking achievements that stirred the enthusiasm of hundreds of millions of workers and others around the globe and left the ruling classes of capitalist countries trembling. These astounding accomplishments include collectivization of agriculture, transforming a medieval system of landholding that had doomed Russia to periodic devastating famines for over a millennium; rapid industrialization that made the USSR an industrial powerhouse within a decade; the creation of a modern army able to smash Hitler’s Wehrmacht decisively before Lend-Lease and before the Western imperialist powers had engaged the Axis militarily. The Stalin-era Soviet Union spread the Communist International, created during Lenin’s lifetime, over the entire world. Communist parties became the main force fighting for workers’ rights and against imperialism in the colonial empires of the western capitalists. Within the Soviet Union great advances in rights for women, social welfare benefits for the working class, and anti-racism, were made. These tangible benefits inspired workers around the world to fight for similar reforms in their own countries. The Stalin leadership did all this while exposing and defeating a widespread network of conspiracies led by prominent Party and military leaders and guided from abroad by Leon Trotsky, a network that collaborated with Germany and Japan to overthrow the Soviet government. Thanks to the avalanche of documents from formerly secret Soviet archives we know today that Leon Trotsky, the Khrushchev regime, and the Gorbachev-Yakovlev regime, lied about Stalin and the Stalin era to an extent no one had previously imagined. Why did this happen? What were the errors of this earth-shaking movement, the process that ultimately led to the reversal of the fight for socialism and communism? Whatever they were, they must have begun during the Stalin period if not before that. Marx, Engels, and Lenin had no blueprint for building socialism in a largely peasant country like Russia, devastated by the losses of the First World War, the Civil War against the Whites and the capitalist interventionists, the destruction of much of its industry and agriculture, a serious famine, and an equally serious typhus epidemic. Soviet leaders had counted on help from revolutions in more industrially advanced Western Europe, but these had been defeated. The Stalin policy offered the answer. Under communist leadership the Soviet working class would complete the task that had taken centuries in the capitalist world, the creation of large-scale agriculture and a modern industry. And they did it! But countervailing forces were at work in the Party. On Stalin’s death they assumed control. The end result, 35 years after Khrushchev’s speech, was the orchestrated death of socialism and the collapse of the Soviet Union and the communist bloc. What we need is a series of detailed, evidence-based studies of the Lenin and Stalin periods to uncover the mistakes that led ultimately to Khrushchev, Gorbachev/Yakovlev, and the demise of socialism and the communist movement of the 20 th century. Although far from sufficient, the works of Stalin are necessary for such an inquiry. -Grover Furr is the author of many works on Soviet history, notably Khrushchev Lied and Trotsky’s Amalgams. His latest book co-authored with Vladimir Bobrov is Trotsky’s Comintern Conspiracy – the Case of Osip Pyatnicky (2024). articles.title: Pentagon Announces Plan To Launch ‘Autonomous Warfare Command’ To Leverage ‘Super Intelligence’ In Warfare
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By John Weeks October 1, 2026 Antiwar.com The command would oversee the military’s expanding use of drones, robotics and AI. US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Wednesday announced plans to create a new four-star combatant command to leverage AI in warfare. During a “State of the Force” address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia, Hegseth said the Autonomous Warfare Command (AUTOWARCOM) would be tasked with scaling “autonomous and robotic capabilities across the Joint Force in the fastest peacetime shift in modern military history.” The Pentagon intends to launch AUTOWARCOM by October 2027, but it will need to secure Congressional approval to do so. If approved, AUTOWARCOM will become the military’s 12th combatant command. The last new command was US Space Command , launched in 2019 under the first Trump Administration. AUTOWARCOM will coordinate drones, robotics, artificial intelligence, and autonomous weapons platforms across the military. It will work to expedite acquisition and deployment of new technologies and seek to make autonomous warfare a central military doctrine. Hegseth said the necessity of the new command was made clear by the Russia – Ukraine war and its proliferation of low-cost drones in combat. “Today, with…Autowarcom …we institutionalize — and we supercharge — the era of [super intelligence], robotics and autonomous systems, all in order to win,” Hegseth said. Pentagon critics have taken the War Department to task for continuing to field extremely expensive platforms, such as aircraft carriers , that are increasingly useless in a modern battle. Hegseth’s speech implied that the Pentagon would continue to field such platforms but also explore modern systems. According to the War Department , Hegseth “announced that he has directed the direct reporting portfolio manager for unmanned systems to lead ‘Project Agincourt,’ an organization that will establish the pathway for [AUTOWARCOM], as well as to execute the existing unmanned systems mission while prototyping a new acquisition model.” He also promised that through Project Meridian, “the Pentagon’s chief technology officer would partner with members of the private sector to study the future of warfare.” PHOTO: US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth gives a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, September 30, 2026, in Quantico, Va. articles.content: By Brett Wilkins October 2. 2026 Consortium News One Palestinian from Gaza said the imagery “shows you the Israeli barbarism and terrorism that the world lets happen.” Updated Google satellite imagery shared on social media provides a new perspective on the staggering scale of Israel’s obliteration of the Gaza Strip, showing entire neighborhoods reduced to rubble and vast stretches of a formerly dense urban landscape transformed into barren wasteland. The images from Google — which is accused of complicity in the Gaza genocide — can be viewed on both Google Earth and Google Maps and show extensive destruction throughout the Palestinian territory. In some locations, roads and familiar landmarks remain visible amid enormous fields of gray rubble where homes, businesses, schools and other civilian structures once stood. “I’ve walked through much of the destruction in Gaza myself, but I couldn’t bear looking at the map,” Palestinian journalist Abubaker Abed posted on social media. “It shows you the Israeli barbarism and terrorism that the world lets happen.” “I’ve been to those places, I have seen the scale of the destruction — it was really heartbreaking,” Abed told The New Arab. “But when you see all the destruction in just one active website, it really broke my heart. I couldn’t even bear continuing looking at that because seeing the place where I grew up, seeing the place where I was born, [lying] in ruins in that way was absolutely heart-shattering.” U.S. writer Linda Mamoun noted that “Google Maps shows photos and reviews for thousands of places in Gaza that don’t exist anymore. You can scroll through an entire world that Israel destroyed.” The Google images help affirm independent assessments documenting the extraordinary scale of Gaza’s destruction. According to the United Nations Satellite Center (UNOSAT), 201,290 structures — or approximately 82 percent of all structures in Gaza — had sustained damage as of June. Rafah. Israel ignored a May 2024 order from the International Court of Justice to “immediately halt” its assault on the city of approximately 275,000 people, as well as other acts enumerated in Article II of the Genocide Convention. articles.title: NATO chief says ‘no imminent danger’ but rearmament of Europe continues in full swing
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Ana Vračar September 30, 2026 Breakthrough News Armament talks continue in Brussels as European leaders pursue increasingly tense anti-Russian discourse and claim “hybrid threats.” More rearmament talks are underway in Brussels as European politicians continue building an increasingly tense anti-Russian discourse. On Wednesday, September 30, defense ministers and industry representatives joined the Euronews Defense and Space Summit , focusing on the bloc’s growing defense expenditure and member cooperation. The summit took place after weeks of allegations of hybrid attacks on EU members, which pushed the already tense rearmament narrative permeating the European political establishment up a couple more notches . It also followed, by only a couple of days, the Council of the EU’s announcement of the next phase of five European Defense Projects of Common Interest (EDPCIs) – projects that “allow EU countries to work together on major defense initiatives that are too large or too complex for individual countries to develop on their own.” While separate, the two events shared several points in common, starting with a focus on increasing coordination between EU countries to arm more efficiently – and spend the billions of euros planned for defense over the coming years. They also emphasized sections of the military sector to receive the most attention – including drones and military capacities in Eastern Europe. This geographical focus goes beyond EU members, expanding to – at least – Ukraine and Moldova. Most EDPCIs – like the Drone and Counter-Drone European Resolve (DECODER) and the Eastern Flank Watch – list Ukraine as a partner. Ukrainian arms entrepreneurs were also present at the summit in Brussels, including leading figures from Fire Point, one of the country’s most prominent arms companies. Very imminent investments into arms While NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated in his summit intervention that there is “no imminent danger” to the alliance members’ territories, he and others did not hold back in offering anticipations of an unstable period. Belgian Minister of Defense Theo Francken, for one, anticipated “more hybrid threat actions” and an overall “dark winter for Europe” – a scenario he seems to want to address by spending more on arms and cutting social services, as he has explicitly stated on numerous occasions. “Europe has been very good in investing in soft power, in social security,” Francken said. “And it’s beautiful to have a pension system, to have social welfare systems when someone gets sick, when somebody loses his job – we have everything. But when there’s a war or there’s hybrid threats, we don’t have anything.” Considering the significant amount of money European countries have already invested into armament, his assessment that “we don’t have anything” is inaccurate at best. It also remains contested on a regular basis on the streets of many European cities, where trade unions, students, and peace movements continue to protest against austerity budgets that aim to provide for war. Europe needs a policy that builds security with its neighbors In addition to large-scale demonstrations against social security and labor cuts in France’s proposed 2027 budget and student strikes against conscription in Germany last week, mobilizations are expected to grow over the coming months – including an international youth strike in November. “We reject the militarization of our societies and support the young people who are refusing it,” the Stop ReArm Europe coalition wrote on September 23. “Thousands of high school students and university students across Europe are rising up to refuse militarization and the return of conscription.” “Nearly 20 million children in the EU – one in four – live at risk of poverty or social exclusion,” the group added. “Meanwhile, governments have committed to military spending that the EU’s own Defense Commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, puts at €7 trillion by 2035.” “The trillions earmarked for militarized security will leave us staring down the barrel of a gun and indebted to global financiers,” Stop ReArm wrote, calling for a solidarity- and care-based alternative. “This must go hand in hand with a non-aligned foreign policy that resolves conflicts through diplomacy, upholds international law and human rights, and builds common security for all: security with our neighbors, not against them.” PHOTO: The Euronews Defense and Space Summit. (Source: Andrius Kubilius/X) The post NATO chief says ‘no imminent danger’ but rearmament of Europe continues in full swing appeared first on MLToday .

articles.title: Ice Age
articles.author: Unai Montes-Irueste
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Industrial Revolution arrived in a natural world that was still intact. AI is arriving while the climate is already making it harder to meet our most basic needs, and while fossil fuel companies, polluters, and unreliable politicians have already ensured too many people lack equitable access to water, food, shelter, electricity, and healthcare. Add AI and it gets worse. Why keep a call center of workers answering credit-card complaints when a bot can do it? Why hire and train a human being anywhere to do anything an LLM or a swarm of agents can do instead? People will die from this, and not because of bioweapons, the parlor game pundits love. They’ll die because they lose their jobs and don’t survive the loss. The fastest-growing group of unhoused Americans is 55 and older, too young to retire and too old to get hired, and their life expectancy drops accordingly. Some of that will be the price of record corporate profits. That’s the bad news. Here’s the good. Deer survived the Ice Age. So did bears and rabbits. So did enough of our ancestors that we’re here to talk about it. They didn’t make it through on individual brilliance. Related: Southern California Edison Is a Predatory Corporation Getting Rich Off a Basic Human Need Late in the Ice Age, the climate’s long stability broke. Freeze and thaw cycles accelerated, coastlines and food sources shifted twice in a single lifetime, and species built over hundreds of thousands of years for one way of surviving were caught flat-footed. Evolution writes its updates over many generations. When the world changes faster than that, the animals who rely on instinct alone disappear. Humans had something else: brains built to improvise a new behavior and teach it to everyone almost immediately, through language, imitation, and story. One person learns to keep a fire going, and within a generation the whole group knows how. That’s a technology upgrade delivered at the speed of culture rather than genetics. We didn’t out-evolve the Ice Age. We out-learned it. And we did it together. Ice Age bands traveled long distances to trade, find partners, and meet other bands at seasonal gatherings that worked like a regional safety net. If your hunt failed, a neighbor took you in. Hoarding mammoth meat was treated as close to a crime, because everyone eating meant everyone survived the next lean week. None of it ran on genius. It ran on teaching. Archaeologists can trace, layer by layer, an elder beside a child at a flint-knapping site, handing over a cheap stone to practice on, correcting a grip, letting failure turn into skill. Children got scaled-down, working tools. Women ran vast stretches of the infrastructure, from hide processing to waterproof seams to the plant medicine that brought down a fever. Elders were the group’s memory, able to say, this happened forty winters ago, and here’s what we did . When a hunter shattered a leg, the community didn’t discard him. It moved him closer to the fire, where his job became remembering. All of it was stored in story, told aloud, around a fire, by an elder, with the explicit job of keeping everyone alive. The Gwich’in tell of a time when humans and caribou were one being, a story that doubles as law against waste and hoarding. The Inuit tell of Sedna, who withholds the sea’s bounty until the community airs whatever it’s hiding, a mandate for the transparency a winter camp needs to survive itself. Don't gloss over this part. This is the sticking point. Byung-Chul Han draws the distinction. Narrative told around a real fire binds people to one another. What we have now is “storyselling,” narrative repurposed to move product and hold attention. A screen doesn’t gather people. It separates them into an audience of one, at scale. Look around. Kids on Chromebooks in underfunded public schools, and kids at $50,000-a-year private schools, are converging on the same picture: a child and a screen. We swipe to date. We blow through hundreds of Shorts and Reels in a sitting. We watch a show while scrolling a second screen, present for neither. Nothing in real life delivers dopamine at the algorithm’s rate, so real life keeps losing. Related: AI Slop, Collective Amathia, and the Digital Dark Age AI accelerates the trade. It sorts our inbox, which lets us send more email, which makes us need an AI to sort our inbox. It’s productivity inflation, with fewer and fewer humans touching the work as it moves from machine to machine. And because AI runs on a compressed copy of what we already made, it’s a photocopy of a photocopy. Errors get duplicated until they outnumber the truth, and the copy becomes the canon. Meanwhile, our hunger to be together has been identified and monetized. During COVID we were desperate to gather, and the moment everything reopened, the price of gathering went up: ballgames, movies, World Cup tickets. Even the humblest gathering is eroding. Thanksgiving tables are getting smaller, because the person who hosted has died, or the plane ticket, the turkey, and the fixings cost more than one person can absorb. Nobody Zelles each other for Thanksgiving. If the host can’t afford it, there’s no meal. The version of the future the tech billionaires are selling features AI actors eating AI food and having AI conversations, while we sit quietly, dangerously lonely in the real world. It’s worse than the Matrix, where at least you can take a pill and find the world outside the machine. In their vision, there is no outside. Their longtermism, with its Mars colonies, private enclaves, and digital successors, excuses present-day neglect of public health, housing, and climate. It treats the current human era as a stepping stone and justifies underinvesting in the institutions that actually hold us together. And the whole glowing architecture will eventually go dark. A cyberattack or catastrophic outage will take down schools, businesses, and every feed that owns your attention. When no one can remember a phone number, and the old wisdom has been scanned and shredded in the name of efficiency, imagine where we'll be. So what do we do? The answer is written into us. When young people engage with elders and ask, "Why not?" The question is answered. Utopian thinking must be recognized as both the fire we gather around and a discipline rather than dismissed as naïveté We must imagine the place we actually want to reach and build toward it, instead of waiting for catastrophe to force us there. We are not short on wealth, talent, or renewable resources. We can thrive if we put community above productivity inflation and AI saturation. If we can admit that the privatization of public knowledge was a choice, then what was chosen can be unchosen. Related: From El Paso to ICE: When Anti-Immigrant Hate Becomes Government Policy This starts with our schools, which need to return to the fire. Kids from K-12 through college need elders, not AI pretending to be one. They need to apprentice the way an Ice Age child did: practicing and failing under supervision, corrected by a human hand. This also means treating teachers like professionals capable of creating their own lesson plans, and customizing curricula. No more scripted classrooms. No more teaching to the test. Kids need to read whole books. And those who are struggling to read need IEP teams who can meet that child's needs, not force feed them cookie cutter, vendor provided, AI-slop. A bot has no stake in a child's well-being. But we do. We still have, for now, elders who remember the world before the algorithm and the search bar, who found a book with a card catalog because that was the only way. That’s not nostalgia. It’s a living archive of judgment that wasn’t outsourced to a machine, and it vanishes the day the last person who holds it does. We should be apprenticing children to those elders on purpose, right now. Stopping the data centers and breaking up the tech companies is the first step. The next step is reinvesting in an analog world. California just passed a bill to bring local newspapers back to life. Hire young people to work for them. We have a shortage of people who are paid good wages to help those forced into homelessness. Change that. Elders need care. Children need care. Plenty of places need cleaning. Plenty of homes need fixing and building. Pay young people to do all of this work, and more. We must make permanent what we already proved possible during the COVID-19 pandemic: direct cash assistance, rent forgiveness, eviction moratoriums, and debit cards so kids could eat. We need more libraries and librarians, and professionals supporting the success of children and youth who work with families rather than around them. We know we need to guarantee the basic needs and human rights of housing and healthcare, supported by people whose well-paid jobs are to get and keep others housed and healthy, and neighborhoods stitched together with libraries, transit, and business corridors, not carbon copies of corporate retail storefronts and fast food franchises. There's no such thing as community if there's no corner store. There's no such thing as Main Street without a mom and pop shop. We are ecosystem creatures, human and natural, and we have to invest in both. No more cities full of waste. No more beaches with private entrances. No more threats to our water — in Flint or from fracking, in runoff from factory farms, or from plastics and PFAS. No more private land ownership of countless acres by British or Saudi royals, or ranch owners, mine owners, churches, corporations, or billionaires. By saying "No!" to the handful of companies that want to insert AI into everything so that every student, worker, and retired person must accept and use it, we give ourselves permission to say "No!" to every form of hoarding everywhere. Related: AI Is the New Plastic Let’s flip the switch. Let’s pick human beings. What we’ll find, if we try it, is that we innovate more and build things that last when we’re motivated by collaboration instead of competition — when not everything is a race to file a patent, especially since LLMs proved that individual copyrights are meaningless to tech-bro corporations backed by world governments and unscrupulous billionaires. Collective. Collaborative. Shared. That’s what we need in K-12 and in higher education. That’s what we should want for the future of work, in the private, nonprofit, and public sectors alike. What actually got humanity through the Ice Age wasn’t a smarter individual. It was a culture organized, on purpose, around valuing community over the individual — one that elevated the people, women and elders especially, who did the quiet, essential work of holding the group together and passing its knowledge on, hand to hand, around the fire where folks came together to break bread and share stories, not through a device. We’re still here because our ancestors chose each other. That hasn’t stopped being the answer.

articles.title: Blessed Are the Peacemakers
articles.author: Walter G. Moss
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In The Sermon on the Mount Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). In 2025, President Donald Trump thought he should receive the Nobel Peace Prize, and in a December 2025 interview with Politico, Trump said this, “I settled eight wars . . . I mean, I settled one . . . one that was going on for 36 years. Uh, I settled Pakistan and India. I settled so many wars. I’m very proud of it. And I do it pretty routinely, pretty easily. It’s not hard for me to do. It’s what I do. I make deals.” In early October 2026, he repeated his claim . He also stated that he “stopped maybe the total obliteration of the world because Iran will never have a nuclear weapon” and that “Obama got it [an earlier Nobel Peace Prize], and he didn’t do anything.” He also quoted last year’s winner, Venezuelan politician María Corina Machadoin, “There’s never been anybody in the history of the Nobel Prize that deserves it more [than Trump].” Despite these words, however, the 2026 prize was awarded to South Africa’s Navi Pillay, a former U.N. human rights chief and judge at the International Court of Justice. Trump’s reaction, according to The Washington Post, was that he “should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t. This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such an [sic] disgraceful and embarrassing decision.” Related: Israel's Conscientious Objectors Stand on the Shoulders of Giants What the world needs now, however, is a leader who understands peace and genuinely wants it, not one who suggests war and is indifferent to the horrors of it, at least as they affect people of another nation. A dozen years ago, I wrote “Where Is the Passion for Peace? ” In it I cited writer and pacifist Wendell Berry’s Blessed Are the Peacemakers: Christ’s Teachings About Love, Compassion and Forgiveness . The question of “where” today is the same as it was twelve years ago. Note this is a different query than “Where Is the Passion for the Nobel Peace Prize?” Although Trump has displayed that, no leader who can write --as Trump did about Iran in April 2026--"a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again. I don’t want that to happen, but it probably will.” No such leader can be considered a true peacekeeper. Especially one who expressed no remorse about U. S. participation in the bombing of an Iranian school in the city of Minab , which killed more than 100 schoolchildren. Or one who makes a deal with Russia’s Vladimir Putin for diesel oil that Ukrainian President V ladimr Zelensky says woud play into Putin’s hands and prolong the Russo-Ukrainian War , which has been going on for four and a half years, about as long as WWI. The combined casualties (wounded and dead) of this recent war are apparently well over one million people--and close to two million . For what this means, one thinks of the words in Ian McEwan’s novel Black Dogs (1993) about World War II in Europe, that it was “a multiplicity, a near-infinity of private sorrows, as a boundless grief minutely subdivided without diminishment among individuals who covered the continent like dust. For the first time he sensed the scale of the catastrophe in terms of feeling; all those unique and solitary deaths, all that consequent sorrow, unique and solitary too, which had no place in conferences, headlines, history, and which had quietly retired to houses, kitchens, unshared beds, and anguished memories.” One also thinks of what Kenneth Boulding once wrote , “Peace is ploughing and sowing and reaping and making things and . . . getting married and raising a family and dancing and singing and opera.” War, however, is too often the killing or maiming of innumerable loved ones, whether adults or children, and the destruction of homes and communities. Today, as we look at Ukraine, Gaza, Lebanon, Sudan, some of us can imagine “all those unique and solitary deaths,” and we wonder if leaders like Trump, Putin, and Netanyahu imagine them. We doubt it. They lack a quality necessary for peacekeeping-- moral imagination . It seems rare for such political heads of state to possess such imagination and empathy. One possible exception was Germany’s Willy Brandt, who from 1957 to 1972 was in succession mayor of West Berlin, West German foreign minister, and then chancellor. In his A Peace Policy for Europe (English trans., 1969), he wrote: “The will to peace and to reconciliation is the primary idea and the foundation stone of our foreign policy.” And in the lecture he gave for winning the 1971 Nobel Peace Prize, he said something similar: “This is precisely the time for me to clearly emphasize my principles: War must not be a means to achieve political ends. Wars must be eliminated, not merely limited. No national interest can today be isolated from collective responsibility for peace. This fact must be recognized in all foreign relations.” If political leaders seem too ready to go to war, perhaps we should look to private citizens or religious leaders for more readiness to avoid or end wars. Both Pope Francis and Pope Leo have expressed the belief, as Leo stated it, that “War is never holy; only peace is holy, because it is willed by God.” Unfortunately, not all religious leaders share such a sentiment. Yet, there are encouraging examples of private citizens seeking peace. Besides those advocates of non-violent approaches, like Gandhi, Martin Luther King, Jr., and former Congressman John Lewis, there are non-governmental people who even during our present wars seek peaceful relations with their nation’s perceived enemies. Two such are Israel’s Jonathan Dekel-Chen, the father of a man who was shot and kidnapped from a kibbutz in October 2023 and held hostage by Hamas for almost 500 days before his release; and Gaza Palestinian Jaser Abu Mousa, who in post-October-2023 Israeli airstrikes lost his wife, two of his children, and his mother. The two men are seeking dialogue across their political divide. ( “Dialogue,” as opposed to war, was also an important alternative to Pope Francis. ) As Dekel-Chen proclaims , “We don't have the luxury of leaving a better tomorrow to our political leadership, to ideologues on both sides. If we continue to wait for this or that political leader to lead us out and to put aside the mobilization of hate for political reasons, then Jaser's children, my children and now grandchildren will be in a very similar situation not too long from now. If we can find a way to have reasonable conversations about how we can make life better for our communities by defusing hatred that has plagued us all for so long,” then such dialogue can lead to peace. Abu Mousa added that although his pain and grief were very real, he learned “to point them at the right direction,” and he turned to advocating dialogue rather than war because of his two remaining children - he didn’t want them to inherit his anger. He believes that when Hamas attacked the Israeli kibbutz they did not see human beings, and when Israel bombarded Gaza, they also did not see human beings. Instead, in both cases, they “took the people as collateral damage or as expendable assets.” What is it with leaders such as Putin, Netanyahu, and Trump? Why do they lack the moral imagination to empathize with the people they see as only enemies?

articles.title: Why John Coltrane Matters
articles.author: Greg Godels
articles.content: By Greg Godels October 4, 2026 For Spencer Weston, who introduced me to the real, authentic Freddie Freeloader I’ve never been comfortable in crowds. I did most of my early serious musical explorations alone, carefully removing the shrink wrap from a newly arrived album, placing the album on our family console, and listening intently as new, challenging sounds swept over me. But I’ve been lucky. I was lucky because, while I seldom went to concerts, I happened to go to three very different, but historic musical events that affected me very deeply: John Coltrane’s performance at the first and only 1965 Downbeat Jazz Festival in Chicago, Woodstock in 1969, and Bob Marley’s last concert at the Stanley Theater in Pittsburgh, 1980. I call that good luck. Of the three experiences, Woodstock aged poorly. The utopian idealism of Woodstock crashed into a wall of cynical capitalist appropriation. The promise of peace and love, the vision of a commitment to tolerance and respect was dashed by crass commercialization and the seduction of success in a class society. Woodstock Nation called for no sacrifice and made no demands, and the participants were coaxed back to taking their places in a society of class-striving and exploitation. As some used to say: Bummer. Within the world of popular culture, was there anyone who so poignantly blended sophisticated politics with a fresh, exotic, and totally authentic musical genre as Bob Marley and the Wailers? Maybe Woody Guthrie. Any group that pioneered, popularized, and dominated Reggae music and ended concerts with a rousing “Get up, Stand up for your Rights” rises well above the mediocrity of the mass of corporate-directed popular music. Marley’s last concert was in Pittsburgh on September 23, 1980 which happens to be John Coltrane’s birthday. This year– on September 23– we celebrate John Coltrane’s 100th birthday. Tributes, memoirs, and appraisals are everywhere. My encounter with this great artist’s music came when I found an album– Coltrane Time — in a close-out bin in the early 1960s. This unusual recording– combining the decidedly avant-garde pianist, Cecil Taylor, an old-school, hard-bop trumpet player, Kenny Dorham, a relatively conventional rhythm section, with the emerging path-finding tenor saxophone of John Coltrane– served as my introduction to the music of Coltrane. Soon, I was anxiously awaiting every release of Coltrane’s new quartet on Impulse! Records. Like Coltrane, the new record company, Impulse! seemed to be dedicated, under Bob Thiele’s direction, to moving conventional sounds in a fresh– dare I say, revolutionary– direction. Looking back, my almost cult-like obsession with Coltrane’s music must have appeared to many as strange behavior for an early-teen, working-class white youth growing up in an industrial oasis among the Midwestern corn fields. Then came a fateful opportunity: Downbeat- – the self-styled authoritative jazz magazine– announced its first (and only) jazz festival to be held in Chicago in August of 1965. Coming off of his greatest commercial success, the majestic A Love Supreme , made John Coltrane a headliner for this event. I talked my friend Steve, a Miles Davis fanboy, into taking a bus some hundred miles to Chicago’s Soldier Field. But to the dismay of most of the crowd, Coltrane and his group did not revisit A Love Supreme . Instead, he and saxophonist Archie Shepp walked on stage playing loud, complex, often harsh sounds. In place of A Love Supreme ’s serenity and contained passion, what we heard that evening was neither serene nor contained. Some said people walked out, though it was difficult to walk out of Soldier Field and leave a continuing stellar program. But people who came to see Big Joe Williams, the blues singer, were demonstrably unhappy. If people paid to be entertained by Coltrane, they were disappointed. For Ammar Kafia, writing in the Guardian earlier in September, this was one of the signal moments when Coltrane cast aside any pretension to conventional “success” and popularity to explore entirely new, risky, and challenging directions. Coltrane’s appeal was never based on entertainment. His work was demanding, challenging to the listener. And those of us who were drawn to his music were well aware of the effort necessary to continue with his project. Yet there was a liberatory character to his journey. Without any fanfare, he revolutionized the perception and status of the African American artist. He liberated the Black musician from the relegation to the night club or bar. His music sold drinks poorly. Long solos and dense, complex music commanded rapt attention and little banter or social drinking. It demanded that he be seen as an artist and not as a cocktail accompaniment. He sped up the transition from bar room to concert hall. He liberated the African American musician from the rigid commercial constraints of the established format of musical theme, followed by the horn and piano solos, and a return to the theme. Coltrane refused to submit to the tyranny of the Artist & Repertoire departments of the recording industry. He made his music, they recorded it. Coltrane redefined the solo– the central creative expression in the genre of what came to be called Jazz music. The recording industry, clubs, and other venues exploitative of Jazz typically imposed conservative temporal and emotional restraints on jazz solos. Coltrane finished his solos when he finished his solos. He exposed raw, intense emotion through unorthodox musical effects. His explorations invariably took him to risky places– sometimes magical, sometimes disappointing, but always impressively daring. Was Coltrane political? Yes, and no. While opportunists like critic Frank Kofsky sought to portray Coltrane as a revolutionary Black nationalist, one could easily see from his interviews how uncomfortable he was with that label. On the other hand, Coltrane penned and played Alabama , dedicated to the victims of the 1963 church bombing and wrote and recorded several Africa-themed works, clearly reflective of his own heritage. He fervently promoted the careers of younger, more overtly political musicians like Archie Shepp. In those regards, John Coltrane reflected his time– a time when the brutal racism of segregation was being successfully attacked and the national liberation of colonies was reaching its zenith. Cultural developments often follow the politics of the time in the same way that the society’s cultural superstructure is largely determined by its socio-economic base. Accordingly, Coltrane’s evolution mirrored the politics of the moment: a country pushing back from McCarthyism, a growing anti-racist movement, the early symptoms of the movement rejecting US foreign policy, especially in Vietnam. Coltrane– like important leaders that emerged at the time– was uncompromising in his dedication to a vision. Like King and Malcolm X, growth, development, and change became a driving force for him. Those who followed King’s commitment closely marveled at how he grew from a fighter against segregation in the South into an opponent of racism in the North as well. How that struggle led him to a broader campaign for poor people and, further, to opposition to the war in Vietnam. Before his murder in Memphis while defending striking workers, King had bravely denounced the cancer of anti-Communism. Struggle led him to a broader, deeper understanding. Similarly, Coltrane’s evolution was unstoppable. From a competent post-bop saxophone player, he came to see further possibilities through his work with both Miles Davis and Thelonious Monk. His near-manic, harmonically-challenging playing– some called it “sheets of sound” — drove critics like Ira Gitler mad, dubbing his music “anti-jazz.” He persevered. Coltrane continued to press harmonic and melodic boundaries, finding inspiration from playing with new instruments, with additional and new colleagues, with inspiration from other, less well-known cultures. He lost fans along the way. Understandably, people with less dedication, less time, or simply less interest, got lost on the Coltrane highway and had to exit, giving rise to grand debates over early-, middle-, or late-Coltrane. Just as many in the early nineteenth century thought that the final products of a sick, deaf man, Ludwig van Beethoven, were a bit unhinged and incoherent, many found late-Coltrane to be self-indulgent and too dense to be coherent. Beethoven’s late quartets are today acknowledged to be among the greatest musical pieces ever constructed. Coltrane’s late works bear serious study as well. John Coltrane, like the great leaders of popular movements in the 1960s, opened up new and daring vistas for millions of people. The times were demanding, and they grew to meet those demands. The post Why John Coltrane Matters appeared first on MLToday .

articles.title: New Reports Show Deadly Side of US Anti-Cuban Policies
articles.author: W. T. Whitney, Jr.
articles.content: By W.T. Whitney Jr. September 29, 2026 New reports amplify call for labor solidarity “You strangle us for forty years and then criticize us for the way we breathe .” Cuban leader Fidel Castro was replying to the criticism, now reviving, of Cuba as a failed state. In fact, destructive US policies over six decades have finally led to humanitarian crisis. Suffering and death rates are up despite collective resilience. Recent comprehensive reports provide information about the origins, substance, methods, objectives, and impact of US measures against Cuba, economic blockade in particular. Two of them appear with support from The Center for Economic and Policy Research (CEPR). Cuba’s Foreign Ministry produced two others. The UN’s Human Rights Councilon September 8 heard Special Rapporteur Alena Douhan’s report on “Unilateral Coercive Measures.” Children are dying Analyst Guillaume Long, interviewed by Prensa Latina on September 15, discussed the US blockade . This senior researcher for CEPR and professor of international relations at Sciences Po in Paris stated that, after 2017, Cuba’s infant mortality rate rose 148% as a “direct result of the U.S. blockade.” He had co-authored a recent CEPR study documenting disastrous effects of blockade on infant health in Cuba and on Cuba healthcare itself. Information in the interview and article apply to the period prior to the US oil blockade and the US regimen of secondary sanctions beginning, respectively, on January 29 and May 1. Infant mortality rates are very likely higher now than as reported by Long. Secondary sanctions are US penalties aimed at third-country companies for dealing with already-sanctioned counterparts. An epochal CEPR-supported study appeared in mid-2025 in The Lancet Global Health, said to be “ the leading journal in global health.” It shows that deaths in economically-sanctioned countries increased in recent years “by approximately 564,000” every year. They attribute the excess deaths to unilateral economic sanctions, imposed mostly by the US government. The point out that, “This is comparable to worldwide annual deaths from armed conflict.” Plus, “children under five years old accounted for 51 percent of the deaths caused by these sanctions.” So that the world and UN General Assembly know At a press conference on September 7, Cuban Chancellor Bruno Rodríguez introducedhis ministry’s annual report on adverse blockade effects. It appears in advance of the vote to be taken October 28 in the UN General Assembly on a Cuban resolution calling for the blockade to end. For 33 years, delegates informed by these reports have overwhelmingly approved the same resolution. The report documents US actions and measures taken between March 1, 2025, and February 28, 2026. It may be ─ should be ─ read here: https://cubaminrex.cu/sites/default/files/2026-09/REPORT%202026.pdf Rodríguez condemned “U.S. policy as an act of collective punishment against the people, with growing repercussions affecting food, electricity, water, health care, education, transportation, and the living conditions of Cuban families.” The Report set the yearlong total of damages at $8,038 billion, a 7% increase over the previous year. It places losses over the decades at $178.7 billion, or $3.897 trillion with inflation. The report cites the US purpose of “provoking hunger, desperation and overthrow” of Cuba’s government. According to Rodríguez, these are words used by State Department official Lester Mallory in his April 1960 Memo on US strategy for Cuba. The chancellor pointed to “furiously anti-Cuban US officials and congresspersons” with “extremely conservative, neofascist ideology” as propelling the blockade. Human Rights Council hears Special Rapporteur’s report The 63rd Regular Session of the United Nations Human Rights Council opened in Geneva on September 9. The US blockade of Cuba was on the agenda for the first time ever. Discussion centered on Special Rapporteur Alena Douhan’s report developed out of her ten-day visit to the island in November 2025. Jaine Zaina Jallad, Douhan’s successor as Special Rapporteur, presented the latter’s report to the Council. In her report, Alena Douhan explores the historical context of US laws, regulations, executive orders and the economic impact of “unilateral coercive measures.” The report covers the blockade’s impact on human rights to food, healthcare, and education. It notes Cuba’s response; aspects of international law; international cooperation and humanitarian assistance; and reduced availability of public services like water and electricity, Douhan concludes in part that, “Primary unilateral sanctions … have been substantially exacerbating the humanitarian situation in Cuba.” She adds that, “The measures in force … prevent, impede, delay or make more costly the delivery of the equipment, spare parts and consumables, food, medicine, shelter and clothes necessary to ensure humanitarian relief and the recovery and sustainable development of Cubans in need.” She explains that, “Restrictions on transactions carried out with Cuba… are all aimed at cutting Cuba off from sources of income. They have resulted in a critical decline in state revenue, hyperinflation, growing poverty and insufficient resources to guarantee the population’s basic needs.” Included among Douhan’s 15 recommendations is her demand that the US “lift or suspend all unilateral coercive measures applied to Cuba.” She calls for repeal of penalties in place for companies that export goods to Cuba containing more than 10% US components, for ships entering US ports within 180 days of having docked in Cuba, and for the use of US dollars in Cuba’s foreign trade. She demands that the US no longer penalize officials in other countries who arrange for Cuban medical assistance. To read the report, go to https://docs.un.org/en/A/HRC/63/29/Add.1 Cuba’s report to the Council Cuba’s government submitted its own 16-page report to the Human Rights Council. This report opens with President Donald Trump’s remark on January 8, 2026 that, “I don’t think much more pressure can be exerted, except to go in and smash the place.” It catalogues assaults inflicted under old and new blockade regulations and repeats information provided by Cuba’s recent Report to General Assembly. It does cover effects of the oil blockade and secondary sanctions put in place after that Report. The May 1 executive order unleashed a “sweeping system of secondary sanctions. These apply to companies, banks, and individuals dealing with already sanctioned entities. “They lead to assets being frozen and restriction of operations of any foreign person or entity in strategic sectors … [such as] like “energy, mining, finance, security, and defense.” Targeting foreign companies, they firm up “the extraterritorial nature of the blockade.” Adverse effects are additive to those resulting from Cuba’s “inclusion on the … [US] list of countries allegedly sponsoring terrorism.” According to this Cuban Report, the US oil blockade represents “an act of genocide, a form of collective punishment against the Cuban people, and a grave violation of International Law, International Human Rights Law, and even International Humanitarian Law.” It states that oil is “essential for the national power grid, drinking water supply, healthcare services, public transport, communications, educational institutions, community services, and every sphere of social life.” The oil blockade is shattering Cuba’s once exemplary healthcare system. The Report cites a World Health Organization declaration saying that that “health must be protected at all costs,” also that the collective punishment now in play violates “Article 33 of the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949.” The Report offers specifics. Ventilators In newborn intensive care units lack “working batteries.” When there is no power, “ventilation must be done manually with uncertain outcomes.” With no electricity, operations continue “under the glow of cell phone flashlights.” A surgery waiting list exceeds100,000 individuals. Some 32,000 pregnant women are “at risk.” Because of raw-material shortages, 300 of the 395 drugs produced by Cuba are unavailable. Without fuel, crop irrigation is nearly impossible and food supplies and donated aid material remain in warehouses. With fuel in short supply, foreign air traffic is down and so too Cuba’s remunerative tourist industry. To read Cuba’s Report, go to A/HRC/62/29/Add.2 or to https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/documents/hrbodies/hrcouncil/sessions-regular/session63/advance-versions/a-hrc-63-29-add-2-unofficial-translation-e.pdf Truth be told US disruptions of multiple sectors of Cuban society have over many years weakened provisions for protecting and preserving lives. Cubans are scrambling to survive. Unprecedented numbers of impaired and vulnerable Cubans are dying. Washington powerbrokers seem to regard Cubans as disposable. Two avenues for the early rescue that is necessary are blocked. The veto system prevailing in the UN Security Council prevents implementation of resolutions approved in the General Assembly. And progressives likely to end US assaults will not soon be holding power in Washington. What remains is international working-class solidarity. Indeed, material aid from all points has arrived in Cuba, items like solar energy materials from China, food aid from Mexico, Japan, and Vietnam, medical equipment from Europe and US donors, and one oil tanker arriving from Russia. But the great need is for oil. Two factors allow for the currently total oil blockade to continue. The US Navy polices Caribbean waters surrounding Cuba. And nations of the world depend on undisturbed flows of fuel and energy for nourishing domestic production and maintaining economic balance. Mexico ’s experience illustrates overall reluctance to disturb fuel-distribution systems by transferring oil to Cuba. International solidarity with Cuba has weakened. Rightwing governments newly in power in Latin America and the Caribbean obey US dictates. Aspirations for continent-wide solidarity, as per Simón Bolívar, Cuba’s José Martí , and Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez more recently, are no more. In accordance with its interventionist 2025 National Security Strategy , the US government holds sway in the region, and Cuba is isolated. In a recent article , Spanish socialist Leire Pajín, member of the European Parliament, condemns US violations of the UN Charter but emphasizes Cuba’s “[v]iolations of civil and political rights.” She calls for “genuine dialogue among the Cuban government, the political opposition and independent civil society … [and] improved governance.” She claims, “This is what the Cuban people claim and deserve … [and] what the Social Democrats in the EU actively support.” What remains by way of international solidarity is working-class resistance to capitalist take-down of Cuba. US labor would be following the lead of organized dock workers worldwide. Off and on for decades, they’ve denied shipments of warmaking materials to zones of conflict. The National Nurses United union on June 30 demanded “an end to the Trump administration’s blockade of oil supplies entering Cuba.” As of 2024, 43 unions and labor councils had already approved resolutions against the US blockade of Cuba. Resolutions are fine, but the need now is for labor action and agitation. -W.T. Whitney Jr. is a retired pediatrician and political journalist living in Maine. articles.title: Improved Medicare for All Will Save Our Rural Hospitals
articles.author: Kay Tillow
articles.content: By Kay Tillow September 19, 2026 Common Dreams At long last, the nation’s healthcare plan will guarantee that not only is everyone covered for care, free at the point of service, but that there is a place within reasonable distance to find that care. After a century of providing healthcare to this rural, southeast Michigan community, Sturgis Hospital closed in June with only 70 hours warning. The hospital was not on the at-risk-of-closing list that had been published by Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) a year earlier. Over 300 Sturgis Hospital employees are scrambling to find work. Registered nurse Beth Kelley , who had worked at Sturgis for 32 years, described the meeting room as filled with “shock” and “devastation” when management announced that the hospital was closing. Nationwide more than 700 rural hospitals are at risk of closing, over half at immediate risk within the next two to three years. The 700 hospitals represent about one-third of all rural hospitals. The termination of care at Sturgis Hospital overloads the nearest city’s emergency medical services. Director of public safety Ryan Banaszak said, “What was once approximately a 2-mile transport for patients has now become closer to 25 miles, which takes ambulance personnel and equipment out of service for a much longer period of time.” The impact is great on Michigan Medicaid patients, who cannot use the closest hospital because it is across the state line in Indiana. “Rural hospital closures lead to significant increases in mortality , and birthing outcomes and obstetric care suffer following closures,” said Michael Shepherd , University of Michigan health policy researcher. The risk increases with every additional mile for emergencies like strokes and heart attacks. A few weeks later the rural River District Hospital in St. Clair County northeast of Detroit announced the closing of its inpatient and emergency services. Four more rural Michigan hospitals—in Mt. Pleasant, Carson City, Ontonagon, and Dowagiac— are in danger of closing with the upcoming Medicaid cuts. Rural Americans live sicker and die younger than those in urban areas. Life expectancy is about three years shorter in rural communities. When a rural hospital closes, the mortality rate rises by 5.9%. Rural hospital closures increase mortality for emergencies such as heart attacks and strokes by about 10%. “There are two kinds of Americans: those who live 12 minutes from an emergency department and those who live 72,” writes Ayla Ellison who grew up in Carmi in southern Illinois. “Whether you survive a heart attack, deliver a healthy baby, or die from something entirely treatable increasingly depends not on the severity of your illness, but on the distance to the nearest hospital,” she continues. She explores the consequences of rural hospitals folding in a country where no one is responsible for assuring help is close enough for a chance at life. The hospital in Carmi closed 20 years ago. Nine more Illinois hospitals are at risk of closure, most of them in southern Illinois. Other states are worse off. In Mississippi, 51% of the rural hospitals are at risk of closing; in Alabama, 52%; in Arkansas, 68%. Dr. Kenneth Williams battled for decades to sustain the hospital (Alliance Healthcare System) in Holly Springs, Mississippi. Rapid expansion of Medicare Advantage plans reduced reimbursement and increased denials of payment to the hospital. In 2023, facing financial desperation, the hospital converted to Rural Emergency Hospital status, a federal program designed to stabilize struggling rural hospitals. The Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) later removed that designation, leaving the hospital again fighting to stay open. Nationwide more than 700 rural hospitals are at risk of closing, over half at immediate risk within the next two to three years. The 700 hospitals represent about one-third of all rural hospitals. That report was prior to the passage of HR 1, the “One Big Beautiful Bill” that slashes $1 trillion from Medicaid. The crisis escalates from grim to disastrous with the looming Medicaid cuts. Federal efforts to save our rural hospitals have been pitifully inadequate in the face of the towering problem. Critical Access Hospitals, created by Congress in 1997, allow small rural hospitals to receive cost-based Medicare reimbursement. The plan was designed to stem the tide of closures. Between 2010 and 2025, 152 rural hospitals closed. Of these, 52 were Critical Access Hospitals. In 2021 Congress created Rural Emergency Hospitals . This designation provides for enhanced Medicare payments allowing rural hospitals to continue with outpatient and emergency services only, instead of closing. In 2023, Sturgis hospital was “saved” by conversion to a Rural Emergency Hospital, delaying its shutdown by three years. Neither these nor any other federal plans are big enough or thorough enough to work. CMS Director Mehmet Oz recently visited Kentucky , home of 35 rural at-risk hospitals. He touted the $50 billion in Rural Health Transformation Funds as the solution. The assertion is absurd. At best, Kentucky will get $1 billion from the rural transformation funds as it loses $21 billion in Medicaid funds . Not even a wizard can turn that into a winner. As Boston University professor Alan Sager notes, no US entity is responsible for sustaining or building or financing hospitals based on community need. “The whole Appalachian area has been abandoned, but its hospitals should be funded and improved, as a necessity of life—like the post office,” says Dare Cima , who is from southeastern Kentucky. With passage of H R 3069 , Improved Medicare for All , finally, the nation will take responsibility for assuring that rural areas have adequate facilities. Hospitals will be paid quarterly, in advance, with a global budget that provides operating expenses. The allocation to hospitals ensures proper staffing with safe nurse-to-patient ratios and optimal staffing for physicians and other healthcare workers . Physician salaries can be included in the global budget. Adjustments to the operating budget will be made “to decrease healthcare disparities in rural or medically underserved areas.” Special projects funds will be used to end discrimination based on race or other underserved categories including geography. Funds will be allocated for construction of new facilities where needed. At long last, the nation’s healthcare plan will guarantee that not only is everyone covered for care, free at the point of service, but that there is a place within reasonable distance to find that care. The late Dr. Ewell Scott , Medical Staff president of St. Clair Regional Medical Center in Morehead in the mountains of eastern Kentucky, predicted that if current policy continued, it was just a matter of time until all of Kentucky’s hospitals east of I-75 would be closed. Sadly, that prediction is breathtakingly close as 16 of east Kentucky’s hospitals in the 5th Congressional District, including Dr. Scott’s beloved St. Clair hospital, are on the list of those endangered with closing by the passage of HR 1. But Dr. Scott was fighting for a different future. He persuaded the City of Morehead to pass a resolution supporting Improved Medicare for All, a national single-payer plan that would cover us all and fund the hospitals. Dr. Scott urged all who would listen to tell their congresspersons: “We know the solution. You’ve got to have the guts to stand up and do it.” -Kay Tillow is the coordinator of the All Unions Committee for Single Payer Health Care, which builds union support for national single payer healthcare. She is also a member of the steering committee of National Single Payer. She lives in Louisville, Kentucky.
